Mr. Speaker,
1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion is prompted by the fact that the public service minister of the province of Quebec has confirmed that 22,000 Quebec public servants hold two permanent public service jobs and collect two salaries during a time of high unemployment. Furthermore, since the federal government has announced that Quebec will get more than $84 million from the Canada Works program for make work projects, 1 should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That this House direct the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to proportionately reduce the $84 million Canada Works grant to Quebec and UIC payments to Quebec until 22,000 Quebeckers are taken off the unemployment rolls by eliminating dual jobs in the Quebec civil service, and if this is not done to withhold the Canada Works grant from Quebec.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of public and private forecasts, including most recently the Wall Street Journal, indicating continuing high levels of unemployment throughout Canada, in view of the general uncertainty in the Canadian economy and considering the fact that the government has promised a statement on job creation in the first week of August and nothing has been forthcoming, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House agrees to sit beyond Friday, August 5, in order to enable the government to bring in legislation to deal with the serious problems of the Canadian economy, and in particular the alarming and worsening problem of unemployment.

SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT LET QUEBEC CONTROL ITS OWN FUNDS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion of pressing necessity.
Considering the economic situation now prevailing in the western world and especially in North America; considering that such a situation affects mostly the American dollar and as a consequence the Canadian dollar; considering the dangerous fluctuation of the Canadian dollar related to the American dollar; and considering that the government headed by the Prime Minister is attempting to hide this situation under the pretext that all these problems are due to the new political situation created by the elections of November 15, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That the government stop fighting in every possible way the Quebec political emancipation that, instead, it concern itself with solving the problems of our deficient economic system which generates the worse ills, namely including unemployment, through a feasibility study to let the provinces control their credit, thus guaranteeing each one's progress.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-MEMBERS' RIGHTS RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gave the Chair notice, as the rules require, regarding a question of privilege relating to the matter we have been discussing. It is a very important matter because it affects the rights and privileges of every member of this House in discharging his or her duty with respect to the obtaining of information to be used in connection with proceedings in this House or its committees.
At the moment there is no doubt that we are inhibited and prevented from discharging our responsibilities because of the order in council which has been referred to. As the Prime Minister seems to be unaware of the contents of the order in council, which are very brief, I should like to read it so the Prime Minister can consider the heinous nature of the document he has laid his hand to. It is dated September 23, 1976, which was four days after a former official of Eldorado appeared in court in Toronto and released a great deal of information after being questioned in respect of this particular issue. The order in council referred to uranium information security regulations, and reads as follows:
No person who has in his possession or under his control any note, document or other written or printed material in any way related to conversations, discussions or meetings that took place between January 1, 1972 and December 31, 1975, involving that person or any other person or any government, Crown corporation, agency or other organization in respect of the production, import, export, transportation, refining, possession, ownership, use or sale of uranium or its derivatives or compounds, shall
(a)	release any such note, document or material, or disclose or communicate the contents thereof to any person, government. Crown corporation, agency or other organization unless
(i)	he is required to do so by or under a law of Canada, or
(ii)	he does so with the consent of the Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources; or
(b)	fail to guard against or take reasonable care to prevent the unauthorized release of any such note, document or material or the disclosure or communication of the contents thereof.
For hundreds of years this House, following the practice of the United Kingdom House of Commons at Westminster, has had the right, under the bill of rights, to see that there is no interference with freedom of speech and debate or proceedings in parliament which ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of parliament. I ask members to contrast that order in council with what should be the uninhibited right of members of this House to discharge their obligations to the people of Canada by bringing into this House documents and material which tend to indicate or touch on the probable liability of the government, members of the government or officials of the government, in connection with any conspiracy, crime or impropriety. Under the terms of the order in council it may well be that we are free to discuss it in the House. But how do we get it here? Under that order in council, as it stands, I am prohibited from finding and obtaining that information in a documentary form and bringing it to this House. I can use it once I get here-but how can I get it
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
here legally? I am prohibited from showing it to members of the public or the media. Under those conditions, how is it possible for me or other members of this House to properly discharge our obligations? There should be no doubt about what took place here, despite what has been said. An extract from what we managed to obtain indicates that on April 28, 1972, a memo was passed from one Gulf official to legal counsel which reads as follows:
Mr. Zagnoli-a Gulf official-remains of the definite opinion that failure on Gulf's part to submit to coercive pressure being applied by the Canadian government respecting Gulfs participation would almost certainly result in severe adverse economic consequences for Gulf, including a material deterioration of Gulfs relations with the Canadian government.
Effectively Gulf is being compelled to participate by the Canadian government.
There is a second memo, dated April 10, 1972, from Mr. R. K. Allen, a Gulf official, which reads as follows:
Mr. Austin advised that a formal declaration would be sought from the cabinet-with the Minister of Justice present-that the arrangement is in the interest of Canada. He further stated that an opinion would be obtained from the Minister of Justice as to the legality of the arrangement in so far as the two Crown companies are concerned.
Because of this particular regulation there is a complete prohibition on the part of any member of the public from taking proceedings in any court in Canada. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made an attempt in consultation with his solicitors who said that in their opinion under no circumstances would it be possible for any proceedings to be launched with regard to a potential infraction of the restrictive trade practices legislation. As a lawyer and counsel of some experience, after looking at a lot of the material, in my judgment there is a prima facie case of breach of that statute. That being the case, the only court left is the highest court in this land-this parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-MEMBERS' RIGHTS RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I understand the government is sensitive about this issue. Not so many months ago the now Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was very put out because of a decision by the supreme court of the province of Quebec dealing with the issue of the restrictive trade practices legislation. I understand why he said what he did. 1 may not agree with him, but it is his right to say what he did. The government is very sensitive and very solicitous about the competition act and the restrictive trade practices legislation. Attempts were made in Washington and in Toronto, and an attempt is now being made in London-at which the Canadian government is represented-to try to obtain some of the facts in connection with this issue. This government has said "no" and has enacted this order in council.
For that reason there is an obligation on this House to make certain that we pass a motion giving us the right to deal not only with this matter in the House but to obtain the documents for the purpose of so doing. For that purpose, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House declare that the order in council SOR 76-644 is not binding on members of the House with regard to proceedings in the House or any committee thereof and that for the purpose of such proceedings, despite the
80020-42(4

The government's purpose in adopting this order in council under Canadian law, after having received advice that the law was correctly interpreted by the government, was to prevent Canadian uranium producers from going under at the same time as the uranium producers in several other countries would have gone under, when the United States government and its economy adopted measures restricting the entry of uranium into their country.
It must be kept in mind that 70 per cent of the world markets for uranium were in the United States. When in the late sixties and early seventies the Americans adopted this policy, it meant for Canadian producers, miners in Elliot Lake and other parts of Canada, that they would have to close down; they could no longer be kept in the production of uranium. A few years later pressure was upon Canada and every other country to supply uranium. We should keep in mind the consequences of inaction by the government at that time had it not decided to act before other countries and the producer group decided to act in order to protect the uranium industry.
This is our policy. It is in order to carry out this policy that we made the announcement and took this action. I repeat, Mr. Speaker-and Your Honour will have to decide whether the time to debate it is now or at some other time-that we want the policy to be understood by Canadians. We are not, like the opposition, putting up a front in order to serve the interests of Westinghouse in the United States.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-MEMBERS' RIGHTS RESPECTING ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

If that is the purpose the opposition wants to serve, that is their right. We will debate this policy when you, Mr. Speaker, so decide. But on this question of privilege, we say there is none. We looked earlier, in answer to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Clark), to see if there was some way in which the order in council could be improved to have any better effect in terms of the right of the opposition to know. We want them to know what is

our policy. We want them to debate it, because we know that the Canadian people will support us on this.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: The question put to you, Mr. Speaker, is the following: In order to debate this policy, do the opposition have to get secret facts of this group of producers, the effect of which will be to serve Westinghouse, U.S.A.? That is the question put to you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Peace River has raised a point by way of a question of privilege of which he gave notice to the Chair, and it is, of course, a very serious matter. I think the Chair should have some time to consider the question, although it is obviously a very timely matter. I must confess that my initial impression is that the terms of the motion are such that the order in council should not be binding on members of the House in the discharge of their duties or upon committees of the House or the House itself in carrying out its work.
It seems to me that this motion reflects the basic nature of the question; that is, that while there may be a potential danger in the application of the order in council to the work of members of parliament, in order to give the motion priority over all other items of business before us there would have to have been in fact an actual restriction and prohibition or interference with the ability of hon. members to carry out their work.

speechtext:

As a general rule, under the unemployment insurance program, all monies received by a claimant at the time that he is separated from employment, are treated as earnings and have the effect of either delaying the start of a benefit period, or are deducted from benefits otherwise payable. speechtext:
1.	Is (a) DREE (b) the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce aware that the October, 1976 APEC report Industrial Incentives Programs in the Atlantic Region states, with regard to existing programs, that "activity under research and product development has been abysmal", that "it is obvious that the region failed to take advantage of research and industrial design assistance", and that "given the region's emphasis on trade, its lack of participation in programs to encourage market expansion is of concern" and, if so, do the Departments agree with such statements?
2.	Do the Departments accept that a sizeable advancement of the Atlantic Region's economy will require major initiatives in product research, development and marketing?
3.	What measures do the Departments propose to ensure more adequate participation by the Atlantic Region in the type of programs cited by APEC?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: DREE-ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is concerned: 1. DREE is aware of the report and believes that increased research and product development in the Atlantic region would be desirable.
2.	Further advances in the economy of the Atlantic region will call for progress on a number of fronts. Viable initiatives in product research, development and marketing would certainly be helpful.
3.	Although DREE does not normally have direct responsibility for the operation of programs of this type, it is prepared to complement and supplement the efforts of the responsible departments with regionally-oriented activities under its General Development Agreements (GDAs) with the various provincial governments. A specific example in this regard is the DREE agreement with Newfoundland providing for the establishment of a Newfoundland Oceans Research and Development Corporation which seek to stimulate the development of marine technology within the province and to foster the establishment of marine ice-related industries based on the technology. DREE's activities under the Regional Development Incentives Act and through industrial development initiatives under the GDAs are also serving to help strengthen the industrial base of the region, thus creating a better climate for new product design and development.
Order Paper Questions
In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: 1. Yes, the department is aware of the statement. The department actively promotes its programs in all provinces, but these programs require an application by individual companies. The use in each province depends on the rate of response of individual companies.
2.	Industry, Trade and Commerce continues to actively promote its programs in the Atlantic region recognizing the importance of both innovation and market development in the Atlantic area.
3.	The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has adapted a number of measures which should ensure more adequate participation by the Atlantic region. Such measures have included a further decentralization of the administration of its programs and the consolidation of a number of the development and incentive programs into the Enterprise Development Program to make them more accessible to smaller and medium-size businesses which play an important role in the Atlantic region.

speechtext: Was the Treasury Board's policy decision to change accounting practices for the 1975-76 fiscal year, as referred to in the reply of the Secretary of State to Question No. 1,059, carried forward to the 1976-77 fiscal year and (a) if so, what is the reason for the substantial drop in the Purchased Repair and Upkeep estimated for the Department in the 1976-77 Main Estimates from the 1975-76 levels (b) if not, what is the reason for the substantial increase in the Purchased Repair and Upkeep estimated for the Department in the 1976-77 Main Estimates over the 1974-75 level before the accounting policy changed?

subsubtopic: EQUIPMENT OR BUILDING REPAIRS IN 1974, 1975 AND 1976
speechtext:
Treasury Board has issued two policy directives to this department relating to accounting practices during the period in question. The first policy directive was in 1975; this directive authorized DPW to recover its costs for certain tenant services to this department; these included the costs of fitting-up new, leased accommodation needed for the expansion of the translation bureau in the Quebec region. In accordance with the procedures provided by DPW and the definition of the Tenant Services portion of Purchased Repair and Upkeep which were affected under this directive, the Department of the Secretary of State estimated $1.7 million as a cost payable to DPW for Tenant Services. That same directive was not carried over into 1976-77; a new directive was issued in early 1976 which revised the definition of Tenant Services. On the basis of these revised guidelines, DPW was directed once again to absorb the fitting-up cost of new, leased accommodation and the Department of the Secre-
August 4, 1977

tary of State estimated that $296,000 would be payable to DPW for Tenant Services, (a) It is this revision which accounts for the sizeable decrease from the 1975-76 figures, (b) The reason for the increase in the Tenant Services portion of Purchased Repair and Upkeep in the 1976-77 Main Estimates over the 1974-75 level is that T.B. guidelines, as per the second policy directive, require that the Department include these costs in its departmental estimates whereas in 1974-75 these costs were included in DPW estimates. It is to be noted, however, that the figure is lower than for 1975-76 since Treasury Board revised the original definition of the cost of Tenant Services. In summary, the figures for the three years in question are as follows: 1974-75 (Tenant Services portion of Purchased Repair and Upkeep absorbed by DPW) $3,000. 1975-76 T.B. issued 1st directive $1,700,000. 1976-77 T.B. issued 2nd directive (but definition of Tenant Services redefined) $296,000.

speechtext:
1.	Did CBC programme "The Fifth Estate" recently carry the results of an examination of news items carried by CBC English and French networks and, if so, did the examination show that (a) 21% of the English network news items were from Quebec and 46% from the rest of the country (b) 63% of the French network news items were from Quebec and only 15% from the rest of Canada?
2.	What are the reasons justifying the low percentage of news items from the rest of Canada used on CBC French network?

subsubtopic: CBC "THE FIFTH ESTATE"
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: 1. Yes. The results of such an examination were carried on the programme "Fifth Estate" of April 27, 1977. (a) The examination showed that CTV and CBC English television network both carried 21 per cent of Quebec-related news during the three week survey period in January and February 1977. CBC carried slightly more Canadian news than CTV, with the two English networks averaging 46 per cent. TV A, the privately-owned French television network, and the CBC French television network carried on average 63 per cent Quebec-related news and 15 per cent news from the nine other provinces and Ottawa combined.
2. In the period analyzed by the Fifth Estate, the French network carried less news from other provinces than the English network. However, it carried twice as much as the other French-language media, namely 15 per cent compared to 6 per cent. The English network serves a diversified society which reaches right across Canada and which generates events likely to be of interest primarily to that society. The French network serves a more compact society, of which 85 per cent is concentrated in Quebec, and it too generates events which are peculiar to itself and are likely to be of more interest to its people. The preponderance of news from other provinces in the English-language media, including the English network, is due simply to the greater interest of the English-speaking public in such news. Similarly the preponderance of Quebec news in the French-speaking media, including the French network, explains the greater interest which the French-speaking public has in Quebec affairs. It is undeniable that the importance of Quebec events, even more than in the past, commands a larger place in the news in the media: the impact of an independence-oriented government in power, the policies, legislation and initiatives of this government produce a steady flow of news both in Quebec, throughout Canada and abroad and it must be treated accordingly. The time and space occupied by these Quebec events have increased at the expense of all other news of lower priority. Furthermore, this situation of an audience
August 4, 1977

comprising 85 per cent Quebeckers, at grips with this major political crisis which it is experiencing so intensely, subjects the CBC and the French-language media to an environment and conditioning which make a major difference in how they treat Quebec news and news from other provinces. Finally, as Quebec is involving all Canada in the most serious and profound political crisis since Confederation, it is natural also that the English-language media should give much more attention and time to Quebec events, especially since November 15. It should also be stressed that it is much easier to gather Quebec news for the English network than for the French network to cover the other provinces. English network reporters seldom encounter a language barrier when dealing with Quebec newsmakers, who are nearly all bilingual, whereas the French network reporters are constantly coping with the language limitations of the newsmakers in English Canada who very often are unilingual. Consequently, it is necessary to take into account the constraints and limitations experienced by the French network in producing its news in English Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the question of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal is as follows: The study referred to appears to be the recently-released report of the UNITAR Conference on future world supply of oil and gas, held last July in Laxenburg, Austria. This conference concluded that additional oil and gas resources would probably be available at least until their use is replaced by renewable energy sources, even if this transition period should last a hundred years or more. This conclusion is considerably more optimistic than other assessments of world hydrocarbon resources. Most of the "new" oil which the conference is purported to have revealed had been known to exist, but most of this oil is locked in our own Athabasca and Venezuela's Orinoco oil sands and heavy oil deposits and the oil shales of the western U.S., and in the still unrecoverable portions of known conventional oil fields. There are also huge but presently inaccessible gas resources in tight rock formations, high pressure zones and other sources unexploitable today due to high cost or lack of technology. The report also suggests that major hydrocarbon resources may lie offshore beneath the continental slopes and deep ocean floor, more in fact than beneath the continental shelves where oil and gas are currently being produced. This concept is purely speculative with no direct evidence available to support it, since only a handful of wells has been drilled on the continental slopes or the deep ocean floor to date and these have discovered no indications of commercial oil and gas deposits. As technology advances and conventional oil fields become depleted, some of these sources of oil and gas will be tapped, just as Canada is presently starting to tap its own oil sands deposits. However, the cost of recovering much of these resources such as those below the deep ocean floor will likely be prohibitive, even with escalating international prices for oil, so much so that other cheaper and nuclear will replace oil and gas for many of their present uses.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council) moved:
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
That this House recognizes the social, economic, environmental and energy issues surrounding the question of northern gas pipelines and, believing that the resolution of these issues must reflect the national interest, approves the position of the government that all relevant reports must be considered before deciding on a pipeline and its route.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I should like to set out the circumstances surrounding the debate in which we shall engage for the next two days. You will recall that we were urged a number of times, particularly by members of the official opposition, to provide for a debate on the northern pipeline issue before the government reaches a decision. Notably, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) on April last, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in May last, and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in May last, all joined together in asking that the House of Commons and its members be given the opportunity to express its views on these complicated questions before a decision is taken by the government.
Therefore, it will be no surprise to hon. members that it is not my intention in this statement to make any announcement
[Mr. Cossitt.J
with respect to a decision but, rather, to indicate some of the issues which have to be considered and some of the problems which are involved in dealing with this important matter. Inasmuch as the government is in the process of considering these problems, the contributions made by hon. members to this debate will be very valuable indeed.
Mr. Speaker, when I participated in the debate on the northern pipeline question in this House on May 13, I pointed out that it raised important issues that had to be considered carefully not only by members of parliament, but also by the Canadian people as a whole. Today I would like to try to provide an overview of the long train of events leading up to the point of decision that we now face and to outline the important considerations-tangible and intangible-that have to be weighed in the balance in reaching a judgment as to which of the various alternative courses of action open to us will best serve the national interest.
As all of us are well aware, Mr. Speaker, the pace of development of the north has accelerated substantially over the past two decades and more, fostered by the expansion of rail, road, air and communication links, the considerable enlargement in available government services, and the rapid growth of a number of territorial communities. Through the early and mid-1960s, the pace of exploration for oil and gas in both Alaska and the Canadian north began to gather momentum. It began to accelerate still faster with the discovery of petroleum at Prudhoe Bay in 1968 and at Atkinson Point in the Mackenzie Delta in 1970.
While most of us have welcomed the quickening pace of northern development, we have also become increasingly conscious of the need to ensure at the same time that such development is in harmony with nature and with the people who live there. In 1970, for example, the federal government issued initial guidelines providing for the protection of native rights, the expansion of native employment opportunities, and safeguarding of the environment and ecology of the north in the event of future construction of oil or gas pipelines. Substantially more detailed provisions were established in the expanded guidelines that were subsequently issued in 1972. In the same year the government also issued a statement on northern development in the seventies which elaborated this concern that industrial growth should be in accord with the people and the environment of the territories.
In the following year, 1973, the federal government announced its readiness to enter into negotiation with the Indian and Inuit people of the north to provide a settlement of claims for the loss of interests that had not been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law. During the course of these ongoing negotiations, the federal government has recognized that a settlement cannot be confined only to material benefits, but also must recognize the aspiration of native people for a much enhanced role in the making of decisions involving their communal life.
In March, 1974, Canadian Arctic Gas filed its long expected application for a pipeline across the Yukon North Slope and the Mackenzie Delta and up the Mackenzie Valley to trans-
August 4, 1977

port both Canadian and U.S. natural gas to markets in southern Canada and the lower 48 states. In that same month, the federal government appointed Mr. Justice Thomas Berger to undertake an inquiry into the social, economic and environmental impact on the north of this project-and of the subsequently proposed Maple Leaf line-which was unprecedented in its depth and breadth.
As the House is aware, late in the proceedings the Foothills group sponsoring the all-Canadian, Maple Leaf line from the Mackenzie Delta submitted an alternative proposal for a line that would carry gas from Prudhoe Bay to Fairbanks, from which it would run southeastward along the route of the Alaska Highway through the southern Yukon Territory, across the northeast corner of British Columbia and southward in Alberta to branch lines transporting the gas to western and midwestern U.S. states.
When it became apparent that this proposal was being given serious consideration by Canadian and U.S. regulatory authorities and, further, that it offered the possibility of an interconnection for Delta gas through a line running southwest along the Dempster Highway, the government quickly established a three-member board under the chairmanship of Kenneth Lysyk, Dean of Law at the University of British Columbia, to launch a preliminary inquiry into the socioeconomic impact of such a project. At the same time, my colleague, the Minister of the Environment, (Mr. LeBlanc), also launched a preliminary inquiry under his department's environmental assessment and review process. As the government has emphasized, in the event that a decision were made to endorse a project along the lines of that proposed by Foothills (Yukon), further socioeconomic and environmental studies would be undertaken to determine how best to minimize any potentially adverse impacts identified by the preliminary inquiries.
Now I should like to say a word about the recommendations which have come forward from these various inquiries. Members of the House have now received copies of the first volume of Mr. Justice Berger's eloquent report, which concluded that no pipeline should be built across the Yukon North Slope or the Mackenzie Delta because of unacceptable environmental risks that it would create, and that no pipeline should be built along the Mackenzie Valley for ten years in order to provide time for the settlement of native claims and implementation of measures to provide native people with a greater measure of self-determination. The summary of the forthcoming second volume of his report, which was released late last week, outlines Mr. Justice Berger's proposals for minimizing the adverse social, economic and environmental impact if a decision should be reached in favour of building a line along the route proposed by Canadian Arctic Gas.
The House will recall that the report of the National Energy Board ruled the so-called Maple Leaf line out of contention, as did the applicant, on the grounds that insufficient reserves in the Mackenzie Delta made it uneconomic and unfinanceable. The board concluded that both Canadian Arctic Gas and the Foothills (Yukon) project, with provision for a connecting line
Northern Gas Pipeline
to feed Delta gas into the express system at Dawson, could transport Canadian and U.S. supplies to southern markets economically and at reasonably similar costs.
The board considered that both projects could contribute significant industrial benefits to the Canadian economy and create an equally significant increase in employment opportunities during the construction phase. In the case of Canadian Arctic Gas, for example, the board estimated that over a five-year period 25,000 man-years of employment would be created directly and 220,000 created indirectly as a result of that project. Like Mr. Justice Berger, the NEB reached a judgment that the environmental impact of the proposed line along the Yukon North Slope would be intolerably severe. The Board concluded that the environmental impact of the Foothills (Yukon) line would be acceptable because for the most part it would follow established corridors. It also concluded that that route was preferable from a socioeconomic point of view because fewer native people would be affected, because those in the Yukon Territory were more accustomed to industrial development, and because negotiations on native claims were more advanced than some of those in the Northwest Territories.
It is clear that in reaching its conclusion in favour of the Foothills (Yukon) system, the National Energy Board gave substantial weight to the proposed conditions to preserve Canada's option to have Delta gas connected with the express line in order to provide for its economic transport to southern markets as and when required to supplement declining reserves from conventional areas in the west.
The environmental assessment panel established under the chairmanship of Dr. Harry Hill last week expressed the view that a southern Yukon pipeline route was environmentally preferable to a Mackenzie Valley line. At the same time it emphasized that considerably more study was required in order to devise measures to minimize the environmental impact of such a line, and considered that further information was required to assess the impact of a line along the Dempster Highway to provide access to Delta gas.
The report of the Alaska Highway pipeline inquiry under the chairmanship of Dean Lysyk, which was made public last Tuesday, provides a further valuable insight into many critical factors that all of us must take into account. That inquiry recommended that a start on construction of any pipeline through the southern Yukon be deferred until August 1, 1981, to provide time for the settlement and implementation of native claims.
Regardless of what decision was eventually reached regarding the routing and timing of a pipeline, the report proposed that the federal government make an interim advance payment of $50 million in respect of such a settlement to a special trust account, with the accumulating interest from August 1 of this year being allocated to serve the various interests of native people in the Yukon. In addition, the report expressed the view that no conclusion could be reached about the social and

August 4, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
economic feasibility of a connecting line to Delta reserves along the Dempster Highway on the strength of existing information.
While the National Energy Board proposed that the project company building a pipeline through the southern Yukon be required to provide a payment of up to $200 million to help cover identifiable economic and social costs, the Lysyk inquiry contended that such costs should largely be met through tax revenues. It contended that any company building a line along this general route be required to pay a minimum of $200 million into a Yukon heritage fund in order to compensate Yukon residents for adverse impacts which could not be readily calculated on a dollar and cents basis.
May I say a word now about Canadian-U.S. options. Both Canada and the United States are now faced with the difficult task of weighing all the advantages and disadvantages, all the costs and benefits that are involved in each of the various alternative courses in order to reach a judgment as to which will best serve the public interest of each country. The United States, which experienced a critical shortage of gas during a prolonged period of severe cold weather last winter, faces a choice of joining with Canada in the construction of an overland pipeline that would transport gas from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska to the lower 48 states, of opting for an all-American system involving an Alaskan pipeline and liquefied natural gas transport ships, or whether to forgo any delivery system now and instead devote its resources to development of other energy alternatives.
In Canada, we are faced with a decision essentially involving three basic choices: of approving a system generally in line with that proposed by Canadian Arctic Gas; of approving a system along the lines of that proposed by Foothills (Yukon), with or without provision for a connection for Canadian Delta gas, or of deferring construction of any pipeline for the foreseeable future and either awaiting bigger finds of Delta-Beaufort Sea gas to justify a Maple Leaf route, or concentrating our resources instead on the development of other sources of energy supply.
Perhaps the best starting point for consideration of the factors that we in Canada must weigh in the balance is the need for natural gas as it relates to the national energy strategy. My colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), will be participating in the debate later, but in order to maintain a proper balance of the various factors involved in a decision of this kind I think it is appropriate that I should refer in the over-all context to the question of energy demand and supply.
One of the central goals of that strategy is to ensure that by 1985 and thereafter Canada's dependence on imported foreign oil does not exceed one-third of total domestic consumption. The magnitude of the challenge we face in meeting that goal was clearly underlined by the National Energy Board in its recent report on Canadian oil supply and requirements. Failing the adoption of decisive policies and programs to reverse the trend, the board estimated that Canada might be forced to rely on foreign oil imports to supply anywhere from 52 per cent to
[Mr. MacEachen.l
62 per cent of its oil requirements by 1985, and perhaps even more in the next decade. Such heavy dependence on foreign oil supplies would expose this country to a number of risks which I am sure my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, would like to deal with later.
There are two basic thrusts to the policies we have been developing to restrain the extent of our dependence on foreign petroleum supplies. One is that of greatly intensifying conservation in our consumption of energy. The other is that of substantially increasing the supply of many alternative sources of new energy capacity that are open to us.
The existing reserves of natural gas found to date in the Mackenzie Delta are estimated by the National Energy Board to amount to 5.3 trillion cubic feet, which is a relatively small volume when measured against the high expectations for discoveries that most of us had earlier in the 1970s. Nevertheless, it is the board's view that this could provide one of the cheapest alternative sources of new energy at present available, one that its calculations suggest could supply some 10 per cent of domestic gas consumption for a period of several years. That is almost double the U.S. demand that could be met from present reserves in Prudhoe Bay.
The National Energy Board estimated that Canada could have a requirement for natural gas from the Arctic to meet the prospective domestic demand and existing export contracts as early as 1981 if Alberta strictly enforced its formula for reserving supplies to meet its own requirements or as late as 1985. In the event that it were decided to terminate exports by the end of this year, the board estimated the supply of gas from conventional sources would be sufficient to meet Canadian demand until around 1989. But apart from the effect of such a policy on our relations with the United States, the board also concluded that the adoption of this course could lead to a sharp decline in exploration and discovery of new reserves.
In reaching these conclusions, however, the board also underlined the fact that it was, in its words, "bedevilled by the inability to accurately predict demand and supply .. ." On the supply side, uncertainty is created by the present difficulty of determining to what extent the development of the existing surplus of natural gas from conventional areas is a temporary phenomenon and to what extent it may reflect accelerated development of new reserves in response to substantially higher wellhead prices. On the demand side, there is uncertainty about how the balance may be struck between increased conservation of gas consumption and the development of new markets for gas to provide a substitute for oil or other energy forms. As a consequence, we are faced with deciding not only whether we should build a northern pipeline, but also with considering when Arctic gas might be required to meet Canadian needs.
The tapping of Canadian gas from the western Arctic, of course, is only one of several alternative sources of new energy that we might draw on in the future. Exploration for conven-
August 4, 1977

tional sources of petroleum in the conventional areas of western Canada has, as 1 indicated earlier, been growing rapidly and yielding significant new discoveries. Extensive discussions have been under way for some time with the producing provinces about steps that might be taken to accelerate development of the tar sands and heavy oil deposits, both of which Canada possesses in abundance. Our nuclear power capacity is being steadily expanded, along with the development of new hydroelectric facilities. Exploration for oil and gas is being actively pursued in the eastern Arctic and the deep offshore area of the Beaufort Sea. Extensive research is being conducted into the feasibility of various forms of renewable energy such as that from the sun, wind and tides.
As I suggested previously, one of the important elements that we have to weigh is whether investment of scarce resources in a northern pipeline to open up access to Delta gas, or in the development of some of these other alternative energy sources I have just mentioned, would yield the best return to this country. It may well be that when all the factors are considered, the conclusion that emerges is that our interests will be better served by following the latter course. Before reaching that conclusion, however, one of the factors which we would obviously have to weigh is the possible effect of such a decision in sharply curtailing future exploration in the western Arctic in the absence of any other measures to sustain it.
We are also reminded by the many reports that have been submitted to us that economic considerations are not the only ones that we must assess in reaching a judgment on the issue before us. We must also be deeply concerned about the impact of a pipeline on the northern people, particularly native people, and on the fragile northern land and the wildlife that it supports. In the case of the environment and the ecology, our concerns must be to forgo routes which would have a harshly adverse impact that could not be overcome by any reasonable means, and of reducing the adverse impact of other routes to the greatest possible extent.
It is a fact that if a pipeline is built, some degree of environmental disruption is inevitable. For this, there is a cost that has to be paid, now or in the future. But the cost can be quite high or relatively low, depending on a number of factors. In the next few days of debate I believe those factors must be taken into account. The only basis for sound environmental protection is sound environmental information. Though we know a great deal about many of the problems associated with the construction of northern pipelines, we will have to know a great deal more. If we know enough, if we take environmental factors into account during decision-making, and if we relate those factors to final design and mitigative measures, we can reduce environmental costs to acceptable limits.
I should point out that the El Paso proposal is not without environmental risk to Canada. While the direct environmental effect on this country of a gas pipeline across Alaska would be relatively small, the same cannot be said of the necessary port installations on Prince William Sound and in southern California. These installations do pose certain threats to fisheries resources that may be of more than local importance.
Northern Gas Pipeline
The tankers carrying liquefied gas are not a serious threat in themselves. The possibility exists, however, that increased traffic along the coast increases the possibility of collision with coastal oil tankers travelling to and from Valdez in Alaska. The results of such a collision could be devastating to coastal and marine life. Major concerns with the El Paso proposal, therefore, result not from the pipeline itself but from the necessary ancillary facilities and concurrent transportation methods.

The move of natives away from the traditional ways of life, living in small groups and relying almost entirely on hunting and fishing, is a recognized fact. Before coming to those conditions, I want to remind the House that Canada has two basic interests in pipeline policy. Our primary interest, our primary goal, is to deliver Canadian resources to Canadian markets. Our secondary goal is to help our neighbour and ally, the United States, deliver their resources to their markets.
At the moment, the Alcan proposal serves only that secondary goal. It moves American reserves but it does not move Canadian reserves. The National Energy Board has recommended a route which would bring Alcan within 480 miles of the Delta, and it is imperative that the government of Canada and the Alcan proponents begin immediately environmental and other studies to tell us whether a Dempster connection is feasible. At the same time, the government and the proponents should review and report upon any other feasible route connecting Canadian reserves to Canadian markets. In concert with those route studies, the Canadian government, which has done everything it could to discourage exploration in northern Canada, should immediately introduce clear, firm regulations and effective incentives to stimulate the search for new Canadian reserves.
Let me come to the secondary-although, of course, important-Canadian goal, of helping the United States. The government of the United States may decide to ask for a route across Canadian territory to serve American needs. Naturally, we should respond positively; but naturally, too, we should put a price upon access to our territory, as they, in reverse circumstances, would put a price. As early as 1968 the federal government made very clear that it supported in principle a Mackenzie Valley pipeline. In that year the federal government established an interdepartmental committee which had one purpose only, which was to investigate the possibility of bringing Prudhoe Bay oil through the Mackenzie Valley. It sent the then chairman of the National Energy Board, that so-called independent body to which the government refers from time to time, to the United States to see whether the Americans might be interested in such a proposition. The only consultation in which the government engaged outside its own bureaucratic ranks in 1968 was with the oil industry. No native people were consulted. No northerners were consulted, whether native or non-native. It is certain that no one interested in environmental aspects was consulted.
Two years later, in 1970, the government published its northern pipeline guidelines to which the minister referred in his opening remarks. What he did not say was that those guidelines gave the green light to industry to prepare a Mackenzie Valley pipeline proposal. The Leader of the Opposition has already referred, correctly, to the kind of encouragement which was offered the small businessmen in the north in anticipation of the building of a pipeline right up the Mackenzie Valley. There is no doubt that this paper, which the minister mentioned but from which he did not choose to quote, represented approval in principle for the construction of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
At that time, close co-operation between government and industry was under way in an attempt to head-off all criticism which might crop up in connection with such a proposal, and various government departments, including the Department of Indian Affairs and the Crown corporation, Northern Transportation Limited, maintained that internal assessments of environmental and social damage could be trusted; that the minister could rely on internal studies and internal information

August 4, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
exclusively when making decisions on this matter. Native land claims were not even mentioned in the document to which the minister referred. The minister did not mention it, but the title of that document was "Canada's North, 1970-1980". I repeat, there was no question of establishing any independent inquiry outside the federal bureaucracy.
Most important for the future of a national energy policy in Canada, this approach, so solemnly established by the Liberal government, was directly in line with the continental energy policy which the administration was then following. The Mackenzie Valley pipeline would supply additional frontier oil and gas from Canada which would be sold to the United States for needed export dollars. Government departments were instructed to increase preparations for the building of a pipeline. Only the NDP at that time opposed such a course of action, this selling out of our energy resources in northern Canada, this total failure to consult the native people, this total lack of concern for environmental considerations.
Then we come to 1972 and the general election of that year. In 1972, out of the blue it was announced that the government intended to build a Mackenzie Highway, the purpose of which was asserted to be the opening up of the Mackenzie Valley and the provision of support for the construction of a pipeline. It soon became evident that once again environmental research had been conducted into this proposal either internally or through external sources and that no native communities affected by such a proposal had been consulted; they had been excluded from any consideration by the government in relation to such a proposal. Moreover, the government steadfastly refused to accept that the building of a pipeline would prejudice native land claims. Rather, the administration maintained its continentalist policy of selling off Canadian energy resources to the United States. This was in the context of the 1972 election campaign. The government was already locking itself into an Arctic Gas type of proposal.
However, the election results were not exactly what the government desired. A minority government was formed and the opposition of the NDP to the whole drift of the Liberals totally thoughtless, totally aimless energy policy brought the cabinet temporarily to its senses. Seeing it could not proceed with its Mackenzie Valley project involving the selling out of Canadian energy, the ignoring of native rights and disregard for the environment while still surviving as a government, it appointed the royal commission headed by Mr. Justice Berger. It is no coincidence, I emphasize, that there was a minority government at that time, with the NDP as the crucial variable.
The subsequent history is well known. Because of Mr. Justice Berger's accomplishments, the right of public participation in the work of royal commissions has been solidly established, native peoples in the Mackenzie Valley will have time in which to get their claims settled and an opportunity to shape their economic future. The Arctic Gas proposal was dead-or at least I thought so until a few minutes ago when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) got to his feet. Last but not least, during the course of Mr. Justice Berger's inquiry, the Alcan proposal was born. I should
[Mr. Broadbent.l
add that without the important precedent set by Mr. Justice Berger it is almost certain that the National Energy Board would not have brought in the recommendation that it did, nor would inquiries have been launched into the impact of an Alcan pipeline on affected communities.
The point I wish to make is this: in addressing ourselves to the Alcan proposal-and I am still assuming that even this government will not make a decision in favour of the Mackenzie route in face of the overwhelming evidence-we must recognize what has been done already for the country by Mr. Justice Berger's inquiry and keep its important implications in mind. We must remember that the issue in building a pipeline is much broader than that of the materials and labour involved, important as such considerations are. What is at stake is the entire question of the way in which we choose to treat our northland and those who live in it. We have learned that the future of the north depends to a large extent on what happens during the next decade. That became very clear to anyone reading Justice Berger's report. We need time to allow the indigenous native peoples to prepare themselves for entry into the wage economy; there can be no doubt about that.

The point I want to make is that in saying this we are not turning back the clock or recommending that that be done. We are saying that as a nation we must take a longer historical perspective and that to wreak irretrievable social, economic and environmental damage in any part of our north simply for short-run purposes would be a decision for which future Canadians would condemn us.
All of this, I stress, must be kept in mind in assessing the Alcan proposal. All of this, I stress, came out of the Berger proposal. During that inquiry it became clear for the first time, as I have said, that a route via the Alaska Highway could have considerably reduced social and environmental consequences compared with a pipeline up the Mackenzie Valley to the Delta. Accordingly, Justice Berger heard much environmental evidence on precisely this route. Following these hearings with care, the New Democratic Party soon supported in principle the idea of this route as being essential for future study. My colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt), submitted a brief on behalf of our party to the Berger inquiry over a year ago making precisely this point.
Subsequently, Mr. Speaker, the Alcan proposal itself was officially made by the financial groups who were interested in it. This was followed by the Lysyk inquiry and Dr. Hill's study. They have now verified that such a pipeline can be built with an acceptable degree of negative social impact. However, the important question we now face is whether the pipeline will be built within that acceptable degree of negative impact. For this reason, we must not be pushed or rushed into any hasty construction; and for this reason, also, the crucial recommen-
August 4, 1977

dations of the Hill and Lysyk inquiries must be accepted and implemented as soon as possible by this government.
I want to make some very specific suggestions with reference to this acceptance in principle. First, we recommend that a delay of at least four years be accepted-and I underline "at least four years". In practice, this means a delay of only about a year beyond the time schedule proposed by the Alcan people themselves, a delay which will likely be taken up with unexpected preconstruction activities anyway, according to the most recent and systematic reports which have been submitted to President Carter in the United States. It is important that we take this time to ensure fair treatment for the Yukon Indians and that we should keep in mind that the delay might in fact slightly exceed the four-year limitation. That is why we want to underline, in face of what the government might decide to do, the need for a minimum four-year period.
In terms of the very legitimate interests and concerns of our American neighbours, it is clear from other reports submitted to President Carter that the United States has at least until the late 1980s before Alaskan gas is needed in that country. This gives our American friends additional time to wait for us to do the right thing in Canada in terms of our energy needs, our environmental requirements and the rights of our native people.
The second matter that I want to stress is the need for over-all control of the project. It is clear that additional research must be conducted into the detailed social and environmental consequences of the project, so that appropriate mitigative and preventive measures can be taken. Without this control, the report tells us that the degree of adverse impact on the people of the Yukon would probably be unacceptable. It is, therefore, incumbent upon the government, in the event that it approves, as we hope it will, an Alcan pipeline, to ensure proper control of this project is exercised, beginning immediately, through such a controlling body.
The third question concerns compensation. The National Energy Board recommended the payment of up to $200 million by the company to compensate for social damage suffered by Yukoners. Dean Lysyk has amended this proposal slightly into a definite $200 million for the creation of a Yukon heritage fund. This seems a sensible proposal to us, as it is clear that some form of general compensation is entirely due. Evidence before the Lysyk inquiry concerning the building of the Alaskan oil pipeline, which would have similar impact to the building of the Alcan gas pipeline, showed that during construction of the oil pipeline nearly half the population of wage earners suffered a loss in real income. That, Mr. Speaker, to the people who live in that part of Canada is a supremely important fact.
In learning from this experience, Mr. Speaker, we must also see to it that steps are taken to ensure that the residents of the Yukon-and I stress, also, the residents of northern British Columbia, an area through which a great part of the pipeline will pass-are not subjected to astronomical increases in inflation. I think in particular of food, housing and utility costs, and I will say something specific about that in an amendment.

The fourth area of concern that I want to stress is that an advance payment of $50 million be given to the Yukon Indians at once so that they may start immediately to establish the new institutions they plan following their land claims settlement. We think this is a good proposal and that it is in the interests of all parties in the north and in the south that it be acted upon immediately.
A few words about the employment consequences of the Alcan route. There will be some important advantages to Canada in building this pipeline, in terms of job-creation. With proper control, the Canadian economy will receive some stimulus in supplying steel. I think immediately of families in Welland, Sault Ste. Marie and Regina which are dependent upon the steel industry, particularly the steel pipeline industry. They will get tangible benefits from this decision. Northerners, of course, will have increased employment opportunities. That, too, goes without saying. What I am saying, on behalf of my colleagues, is that through federal government action we must ensure that the probability of increased jobs in the steel towns of the south and increased employment for northerners on the spot become not just a probability but a certainty.
Another advantage of the Alcan proposal is that although it is clearly premature to say that a link with the Mackenzie Delta via the Dempster Highway would be acceptable on the basis of the known evidence, the Alcan proposal does at least offer the potential for such a link in the future when we might require it. Most of all, Mr. Speaker, the Alcan proposal gives the people of Canada time-time to develop a more comprehensive energy policy, and time to consider a balanced and long-term approach to northern development. It has been the absence of a coherent national energy policy that has led to the demands of many for frontier gas at once, in the fear that we were imminently running out of supplies. That has been particularly felt throughout southern Canada. It has been the absence of a coherent strategy for future northern development that has led many people in the north, not just in Inuvik but other communities, to seek pipeline construction as their only salvation. Both of these hastily drawn conclusions are wrong.
The point is, as the Hill and the Lysyk reports make clear, their principal recommendations do not lock us in if we accept them in terms of other possibilities. They give us time to plan, not only for the north but time to plan for a comprehensive policy which is totally lacking at the national level at this time.
I listened with agreement in almost every detail to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) in terms of his proposals about the need for a national energy policy and his criticism of the total absence of one coming from the present cabinet. We need a policy which will seriously deal with energy conservation. The approach of the federal government to this is laughable. The minister knows that a report on the leading industrial countries which was published in the last year shows that Canada and the United States have the worst record in terms of energy conservation policies.

It is a shame that such a policy exists and should be passed off as being credible in the real world. A national policy of some depth would give emphasis to developing alternative energy resources. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has spoken a number of times on what should constitute such an approach. Such a policy should ensure a fair distribution of the consumer burden on higher energy costs, which is totally absent at this point in the national policy. A comprehensive policy should ensure that increased corporate returns, which are now going out in the hundreds of millions of dollars, be directed to the development of additional domestic oil and gas resources for Canadians as a condition for their being maintained. It is a scandal that hundreds of millions of Canadian dollars should be going out to multinational oil companies with no requirement that those funds be reinvested for development in Canada.

With specific reference to the Alcan proposal, which I have indicated we support in principle, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and after considering the evidence and reports of the relevant inquiries, this House approves the granting of a certificate for a pipeline through the southern Yukon as recommended in principle by the National Energy Board and the Lysyk and Hill inquiries, with particular reference to the following conditions:
(1)	That an Alcan pipeline authority be established immediately comprised of representatives of the native communities, labour, small business, consumers and conservationists from the affected pipeline corridor and from the federal, provincial and territorial governments, and that this authority be empowered to manage the regional impact of pipeline construction especially with respect to employment practices, and food, housing and utility prices as well as assuming the other responsibilities recommended by the above inquiries;
(2)	That a "Canada first" priority be enforced in hiring, contracting and supplying the pipeline with particular preference to local residents of the Yukon, British Columbia and Alberta in the vicinity of the pipeline route;
(3)	That no pipeline construction precede a fair settlement of the affected native land claims; and
(4)	That no pipeline construction commence before August 1981, and that the interval be used to inquire further into the local impact of pipeline construction, to determine final route selection, and to control project planning;
and furthermore that exports of Canadian natural gas licensed for delivery to the United States after 1985 be considered as credits to be redeemed from the United States on an equivalent BTU basis."
The amendment concerning gas exports after 1985 would save Canadians roughly 4.1 trillion cubic feet of gas, but would cut off that amount from the United States markets which need it. It would merely require that it be repaid at some future date, at a time when the Americans have an adequate supply to do so, an adequate supply established by the pipeline itself. If we are concerned about Canadian interests in the pipeline, surely this should be a paramount consideration. It is consistent with our already established policy of phasing out oil exports. It gives the United States considerable notice and, most importantly, it will add considerably to

Canadian energy supplies after 1985 and hence to the flexibility we need for meeting our future energy needs. This action should be undertaken by this government whether or not we approve a northern pipeline.
In accepting this course of action which we have proposed this afternoon, we believe Canadians will have an opportunity to rethink our policies on northern development and establish an over-all national energy policy. It will be a chance to step back. It will be an opportunity for some breathing time. We in the New Democratic Party are proud to have been an integral part of this process. The onus is now clearly with the government to seize this opportunity to do future good for the country and, in particular, for the future well-being of the north and its people.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take part in the debate because I believe this is a basic issue which must be analysed so that a realistic decision can be taken in the interest of the nation that we represent in this House. We know that Mr. Justice Berger has suggested that the Canadian government place a ten year moratorium on the construction of any pipeline in the Mackenzie area. However, since the recommendation made in the Berger report, major changes have been brought to the Foothills pipeline project. Whether these changes were postponed voluntarily or not, it remains that the National Energy Board believes that this moratorium is not necessary for the Alcan route since it has agreed to it.
This ten year moratorium would enable the natives of the Northwest Territories to establish more freely their claims and to negotiate without any pressure, as was the case for the Inuit
August 4, 1977

of James Bay. This would also enable Canada to improve its natural gas transportation technology and eventually find other more ecologically safe answers, both for transportation and for our real needs and energy requirements. The National Energy Board has also made an investigation in this regard and its conclusion was approximately the same as that of the Berger study. The National Energy Board also believes a pipeline through the Mackenzie Valley would be disastrous from all aspects. I am in total agreement with this point. The National Energy Board was, however, given its agreement to the Alcan proposal. The Alaska Highway Pipelines distribution system will receive natural gas from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska and will deliver it to the United States.
This proposal was made to meet the most urgent needs while allowing for a better transportation policy for northern Canada supplies to be developed. Therefore, the Alcan route is the most adequate in the present situation and 1 can only support it, even though I have a few reservations. While all industrialized countries are beginning to show concern about the accumulated deterioration of their natural environment, we ourselves continue to exhaust our resources for short term economic reasons and we continue to shatter the harmony between man and his environment.
Mr. Justice Berger showed clearly in his report to what extent the natural balance in the northwest is precarious. I understand that footprints and tire imprints can take up to ten years before disappearing. What will the prints made by 7,000 men, 50,000 vehicles, and so on leave us? Already, in certain areas of the Arctic, the Inuit are catching oil-covered seals, not to mention the animals that will no longer be proper for human consumption, the threatened species, and the risks of irreversible pollution which are more than possible; they are obvious. I think that Mr. Justice Berger's proposal to set up a sanctuary for some species is a necessity if we want to preserve them as well as their habitats. In addition to all the anticipated ecological deteriorations, another matter of concern arose in the minds of the people of the Yukon. Recently, a pump station of the Trans-Alaska oil pipeline exploded. It is only one accident among so many others that the government must anticipate. So steps will have to be taken to prevent this kind of accident from occurring, and in view of the possibility that always exists we will have to come up with top safety systems. One only has to remember how many times this kind of accident happened either at sea or on land. On land leaks and explosions are more harmful, and recuperation is difficult on land. In a few years we will probably start thinking about dressing the wounds that we will have opened in those yet virgin habitats.
It is certainly necessary to develop a minimum of our natural resources but does our export of natural gas to the United States justify that rush for gas dollars? All those who studied the Berger report agree on one point: the construction of pipelines in the north could have alarming effects on the environment and the animal species, man included. In the balance of Canada's future improvement, is the environmental loss worth the economic gain? Because this is indeed an
Northern Gas Pipeline
economic need. The government's commitments to export natural gas represents about 40 per cent of our total annual production. Our consumption of natural gas represents about 80 per cent of our total energy consumption, and it was proven to every conscious mind that our need for natural gas can easily be reduced, and it is quite inevitable that in a relatively near future we will have to make room for renewable energy.
Natural gas is used mainly for heating and several qualified scientists say that in this area of consumption several types of renewable energy can be used. If one looks at the statistics of government grants for energy research and development one readily realizes that for this government renewable energy is not an urgent imperative. In 1976-77, less than 4 per cent of the amount allotted for energy research and development went to renewable resources. The government suffers from tunnel vision when looking at the future and that is why no figure is put on the commercial nature of natural gas.
The current energy crisis will come to an end only when governments realize that renewable energy is the solution we shall finally have to accept. If the reason for this technological dealy is economic in nature, this is only one more evidence of the incompetence of our political magnates. The most important factor in any project which is in the common good, as the building of this pipeline is supposed to be, is the human factor itself. Well, the human aspect in the regions which will be affected by the building of a pipeline will be subjected to heavy pressure due to the fact that a large portion of the population there is made up of Indians. As a matter of fact, it will not be possible to extract one single cubic centimeter of natural gas within Indian territories without damaging an environment which is, in most cases, their only source of income. Moreover, it is also their only reason to live.
Once more this would mean taking control over significant parts of their lands. And whatever the aspect of future negotiations, the result will probably be as usual that the government will assume resource development rights, and the native people will lose access to certain lands in consideration of the settlement of their claims to land they were already owning in any case, monetary compensation. As long as the native people will live on resource-rich lands, they will be up against the big capitalistic machine, and even if there are democratic negotiations, they will end up socialized, with compensatory goods that are foreign to their natural culture.
One point made by corporations competing for the relevant pipeline was that of benefits to native people. There is reference to 4,000 direct and indirect jobs. There is reference to reduced unemployment and minimized welfare reliance. There is also reference to the jobs native people ask for. In fact some do, but others do not. I suggest no one here can state in conscience whether they want those jobs or not, or even whether those jobs will be created. Mr. Justice Berger had this to say in his report:
There is abundant reason to doubt that a pipeline would provide meaningful and ongoing employment to many native people. The pipeline contractors and unions have made it plain that native northerners are not qualified to hold down skilled positions in pipeline construction, and that they will be employed largely in unskilled and semi-skilled jobs. Once the pipeline is built, only about 250

August 4, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
people will be needed to operate it. Most of these jobs are of a technical nature and will have to be filled by qualified personnel from the south.
As I said, suggested benefits to native people are short-term benefits. This in no way resolves that particular problem, nor the language and race problems that are bound to crop up. Seven different dialects are currently spoken in these lands. And I would call on those who know what happened in the early 70's on the Quebec north shore and Labrador to remember the discrimination against native employment. Natives were tied to menial tasks, without any access to better working conditions to which every Canadian is entitled.
Experience has shown me that most native people looking for paid work wanted to earn enough money to buy the tools which they need to continue to lead their own way of living. The Inuit more particularly are proud people who want to assert their independence and self-determination. They have clearly shown it on several occasions, especially at James Bay. 1 do not think that menial work is conducive to the independence of an ethnic group. In addition, if the native people want better paid and more qualified jobs, they will have to learn to speak our language and get some education. This could eventually mean their assimilation by new needs rather than the improvement of their human and social condition. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to insist on the fact that the construction of a pipeline in northern Canada could jeopardize a unique habitat in Canada and our native people. For those reasons, I wish to state my systematic objection to the Arctic Gas pipeline route.
One must chose the lesser of two evils, and as the Foothills Pipe Lines project will allow us to arrive at a better Canadian gas transportation policy for the future, I support it, conditional upon the following, however: That the government see to it that the Americans do not reap all the benefits of the undertaking by letting us shoulder all ecological damages; that the government negotiate with our natives with every consideration they are entitled to as original owners of the territories concerned; that it allow them to assert themselves without imposing upon them a way of life to which they were not born and, as our needs for natural gas are very relative, without imposing any temporal constraints upon them as has been the case with the James Bay Inuit with regard to negotiations; that the government see to it, without any further delay, that all forms of energy capable of replacing more wisely and progressively the consumption of natural gas be considered with a view to meeting social and conservation requirements before political and economic needs; that the government give more importance than it does now to the long term factor so that the energy and ecology situation does not find itself again in a bind in the future; and finally, that the government put off the construction of pipelines in virgin areas of the northwest until such time as all means have been developed to protect the environment, and negotiations with our native people have led to equitable conclusions.
