speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some years now this government, members of this House, and people across Canada have been concerned with the question of pipelines through Canada's north to bring gas to southern markets. Prompted by the tremendous pressure for additional gas in the United States now and the possibility of future increased Canadian demand, the investigation of and discussion on northern pipelines have been extensive and sometimes exhaustive. But now is the time for a decision.
Members of this House have before them the results of the Berger inquiry into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline proposal, the National Energy Board report on the whole northern pipeline issue, the report of the environmental assessment panel on the Alaska highway proposal, Dr. Hill's report, and finally, the Lysyk report on the potential socio-economic impact of the Alaska highway pipeline. In the course of all these inquiries and studies the people of Canada were consulted extensively, and this is particularly true of those living in areas most likely to be affected by any pipeline.
I can honestly say that few issues in Canadian history have received as much attention and debate. This is a reflection of the importance which Canadians place on this issue, and it is also a reflection of the lengths to which the government has gone in order to ensure that, when the time comes for decisions, those decisions can be made rationally and based upon the best available information.
The inquiries that have taken place during the past three years have added a great deal to our previous knowledge of the north, its people, and the impact of possible pipelines along several proposed routes. Let us consider the facts. I believe everyone in this Chamber recognizes that northern Canada is a unique part of this country and that part of that uniqueness stems from its fragile and in many ways very special environment. For many years federal departments, including the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, have conducted major comprehensive programs of investigation and research centred on special northern characteristics, the effects of its vigorous climate, its special soil conditions, its unique wildlife, and how these relate to the culture, lifestyle and aspirations of those native to the north.
All of these examinations, both regular programs and special inquiries, had one objective in common-better protection of the north and better management of its natural resources. But to protect and to manage properly, we must have a basic understanding of such diverse subjects as geology, vegetation, lakes, rivers and streams, wildlife, fish and sea mammals. Gaining this understanding has not been easy-northern areas are vast and funds are not unlimited. Still, we have accomplished and learned a great deal. Canadian knowledge of our northern frontier is as good or better than that of any other nation with large northern areas.
August 4, 1977

In our search for basic knowledge we discovered that the north held significant mineral and petroleum resources. By the 1960's significant petroleum resources had been identified in the Arctic coastal waters and Arctic islands. This was an interesting discovery but one that did not assume major importance until the western nations realized that they had a problem of energy supply. It was then, in the late 1960's, that interest in the development of northern petroleum resources began to surface.
In December, 1968, the government set up a task force on northern oil development and from this arose the special environmental social program-a program designed to uncover the possible impact of a northern pipeline.
The specific aim of that program was to gain the knowledge necessary for the protection of the northern environment and the social and cultural life of those native to the north. Even then it was realized that there had to be a balance between development and the protection of the human and physical environment of the north.
The geographic scope of the program was very broad, covering the entire Mackenzie Valley region north of the 60th parallel, the sensitive northern Yukon slope to the Alaska border and southward in Yukon to include the Old Crow flats.
Without belabouring the point, I want to say that the knowledge we have gained from this program-contained in 270 separate research reports-has been invaluable both to the government and to all of the inquiries that have looked into the question of northern pipelines. The program also led to the tabling in this House on June 28, 1972, of the Expanded Guidelines for Northern Pipelines. The guidelines served to spell out the kinds of information required when a pipeline company applies for a land use permit under the Territorial Lands Act, administered by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand).
Other mechanisms have also been set up to ensure proper development in the north. The environmental assessment and review process, established by cabinet in 1973, requires a detailed and comprehensive assessment of the potential environmental impact of any project involving federal lands or federal money or sponsored by a federal department. The Environmental Assessment Panel, established to examine the possible impact of the proposed Alaska highway pipeline, submitted an interim report to my minister only a day or so ago.
Another important feature of our efforts to minimize social and environmental disruption in the north is the support of this government for the corridor concept. What this means is that we try to minimize or lessen the impact of development by channelling it into one corridor. To fail to do so would simply mean random development with widespread impact in many areas. I do not think we can afford that. It is imperative, I think, that when we consider pipeline routes, we also consider associated developments. These other facilities must, of course, be examined on their own merits as well. As one of the
Northern Gas Pipeline
witnesses before the recent hearings of the Environmental Assessment Panel in Whitehorse put it, we, as a country and as a people, cannot afford wholesale environmental destruction by insignificant increments.
In its support of this concept the government has initiated a number of other programs which have been accelerated to meet the challenge of constantly changing contexts. We are looking at the possible impacts of a pipeline on the high Arctic. Efforts have been made to accelerate the gathering of baseline data in southern Yukon, and we have joined with industry in research on the Beaufort Sea. The end product of all these ventures, whether strictly federal or carried out in co-operation with industry, will be increased understanding of what is acceptable development in Canada's north and where in the north that development should take place.
To this point I have spoken about the environmental and social criteria which the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) believes must be applied in making a decision on northern pipelines. There are, of course, many other factors to be considered which I am sure will surface, or have already done so, during this debate.
However, I do want to emphasize that the government has been preparing for this decision for some time. The Department of Fisheries and the Environment, both alone and in co-operation with others, has been studying the potential impact of northern pipelines for several years now, and more knowledge is being gathered every day.
I would like to turn now to the individual proposals for northern pipelines and mention some of the potential environmental effects of each.
The government is required to make two decisions very shortly. First, it must decide whether or not to permit the construction of a gas pipeline in the western Arctic. Second, if a pipeline is allowed, the government must decide through which corridor it should pass.
Essentially there are two proposals before the government. The first is a proposal by Canada Arctic Gas Pipeline Limited to construct a buried gas pipeline through northern Yukon and down the Mackenzie Valley carrying both Alaskan and Canadian gas.
Second, there is a proposal by Foothills Pipe Lines (Yukon) Limited to construct a buried gas line along the Alaska highway in the southern Yukon passing through B.C., Alberta and Saskatchewan, where it would join existing pipeline facilities. The latter pipeline is intended to carry only Alaskan gas, although Canadian gas could be transported by constructing a lateral line following the Dempster Highway, if such a link were found to be environmentally and socially acceptable.
Another proposal, the Foothills Mapleleaf Line down the Mackenzie Valley, has been withdrawn at the request of the company.
Finally, we must remember the El Paso proposal to carry gas across Alaska and then by tanker to southern markets. While this proposal is obviously not the subject of an applica-

August 4, 1977
Northern Gas Pipeline
tion to the Government of Canada, it may have a bearing on our decision.
All of the Canadian proposals have been the subjects of one or more public inquiries as well as extensive scientific evaluations. The National Energy Board has reported on the three major Canadian proposals. The Berger inquiry has published the first volume of its examination of the Arctic Gas and Foothills Mapleleaf proposals. The Environmental Assessment Panel has completed its report on the Alaska Highway proposal, as has the Lysyk inquiry. I do not intend to pass judgment on the findings of these inquiries today, but these investigations, combined with a great deal of research by the government, have identified the primary environmental concerns associated with each proposal.
Let me deal first with the potential effects of the El Paso proposal. While the direct environmental effect on Canada of a gas pipeline across Alaska would be relatively small, the same cannot be said of the necessary port installation on Prince William Sound. That installation would pose certain threats to fisheries resources which may be of more than local importance.
The tankers carrying chilled gas are not a serious threat in themselves. The possibility exists, however, that increased traffic along the coast increases the possibility of collision with coastal oil tankers travelling to and from Valdez. The results of such a collision could be devastating to coastal and marine life in Canada. Major concerns about the El Paso proposal, therefore, result not from the pipeline itself but from the necessary ancillary facilities and concurrent transportation methods.
The Arctic Gas and Foothills proposals have much more direct environmental impacts on Canada's north. A pipeline along the northern Yukon coast, across the Mackenzie Delta and down the Mackenzie Valley has a very high potential for environmental disruption.
The Delta and northern Yukon are vital breeding areas for many species of animals, birds and sea mammals. There are no alternative breeding grounds which could support these populations to the same degree. Populations of birds that range all across North America, whales that roam much of the Arctic and north Pacific, as well as one of the last surviving large herds of caribou could be permanently reduced.
In addition, heavy construction work necessary for the building of any pipeline could disrupt the biological productivity of the Delta, coastal plain and inshore waters. Such a disruption would have a severely negative effect on the wildlife on the entire continent and on the oceans, even in areas far from the pipeline itself.
Further down the proposed Arctic Gas line, in the Mackenzie Valley itself, environmental problems tend to be more of a geotechnical or engineering nature. Finding stable ground- stable enough to ensure pipeline integrity-is just such a problem. The problem is particularly acute in areas of discontinuous permafrost where either chilling the gas or warming it could cause frost heave or excessive settling of the pipe. There

are also problems associated with ancillary structures such as excessive noise from compressor stations, the construction of access roads and others. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when 1 left off at six o'clock I was outlining some of the difficulties to be reckoned with in pipeline operations such as discontinuous permafrost, the provision of suitable access roads, and so on. However, on a comparative level, the potential environmental problems likely to be encountered on the Alaska or Klondike highways are generally less severe than those on the Mackenzie Valley line. Both of these possible alternatives use existing corridors. The areas through which these routes pass are less critical to the survival of major migratory species, and the region is less biologically productive at the peak breeding season.
Certainly there are difficulties associated with the Alaska Highway route, especially in the first 150 miles. Here there are specific areas containing unique and endangered species. There is a higher risk of major or minor earthquakes here than along the Klondike diversion proposed by the National Energy Board. There is also the hazard of discontinuous permafrost and ice rich soils in this portion of the proposed line. It appears, however, that most of these obstacles can be minimized through effective engineering or by changing the route so as to avoid specific problem areas.
A number of other challenges present themselves. There could be local damage to forests and other plant life. Revegetation in the Yukon is a very slow process. The aesthetic value of the land might be harmed, particularly in the northern section of the Alaska Highway. The access provided by right of ways and compressor station service roads might open areas to larger numbers of people and this could be a definite threat to wildlife and fisheries resources. And in the case of the possible Dempster lateral, both the highway and the pipeline would cross the migratory path of the Porcupine caribou herd. This latter aspect is of special concern to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment.
On the whole, however, the potential environmental problems on the Alaska Highway or Klondike routes do seem more predictable than those likely to be encountered on the Mackenzie Valley route, and because they are more predictable,
Northern Gas Pipeline
environmental protection measures can be more easily and more effectively devised.
The possibility still exists, however, that Canada may need the resources offered by the Mackenzie Delta and Beaufort Sea. The exploitation of those resources will, in itself, bring significant environmental problems. The Department of Fisheries and the Environment has anticipated this and has begun a technology development program to help us deal with potential problems associated with on-shore collection and processing and off-shore exploitation operations. The program is being carried out over a five-year period.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, a great deal of evidence has been collected in the last few years in anticipation of the construction of northern pipelines.

The building of a pipeline involves not only the environment but important economic issues as well. Let me assure you, on behalf of my minister, that the Department of Fisheries and the Environment does strive for a sense of perspective and reasonable pragmatism in environmental issues. It is a fact that if a pipeline is built, some degree of environmental disruption is inevitable. For this there is a cost that has to be paid-now or in the future. But the cost can be quite high or relatively low depending on a number of factors. I believe those factors must be taken into account in moving toward a decision.
The only basis for sound environmental protection is sound environmental information. Though we know a great deal about many of the problems associated with the construction of northern pipelines, we will have to know a great deal more. If we know enough, if we take environmental factors into account during the decision-making, and if we relate those factors to final design and mitigative measures, we can reduce environmental costs to acceptable limits.

Before dealing with the remarks of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) I think it is worth while putting on the record an assurance 1 was very glad to see in the light of the assertion made by the leader of my party. 1 refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on July 28 at a press conference with respect to the ultimate method of disposing of the pipeline question, and I read from page 12 of the transcript of the press conference on that date. As part of his answer the Prime Minister said:
The only thing I think I can safely say is that because of the multiplicity of these reports and because of the variety of concerns which have to do not only with energy and its transportation but with the financial implications, its job creation implications, with the rights of the native peoples in the North, and with the environment-they have to deal obviously with the problem of foreign affairs in relation to the United States-because of this complexity it is inevitable that if we do build a pipeline, it will have to be by legislation. In other words, we will have to come to parliament with a law saying that A, we are building the pipeline and, B, this is the route, and, C, this is what we will do with respect to financing and, D, there are the measures we are taking for the environment and E, this is the kind of contract we are making with the United States. I am just making the point that it would be a very complex series of decisions which I think would be best debated by parliament and therefore would be placed in the form of legislation, if we decide to build a pipeline.
That is the first definitive and positive statement which has appeared with respect to this subject matter finding its ultimate form by way of legislation before this House. So once a decision is made-and it is anticipated one will be made next week, possibly next Monday-we look forward to the honouring of that commitment by the Prime Minister to see that there is a debate here before a pipeline is built.
Having sat here as long as I have, I was disappointed to see the Prime Minister leave the Chamber before the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) had completed his comments and before the Leader of the New Democratic Party and the spokesman for the Social Credit Party had delivered theirs. It was a hollow comment on the assurance given to us by the President of the Privy Council that the views of parliamentarians in this, to my mind, rather useless and meaningless debate, will be taken into account. The hon. gentleman said they would be given careful consideration, but 1 know the Prime Minister does not waste his time reading the comments of the leader of the NDP or of the spokesman for the Social Credit Party. However, his attitude serves to draw attention to the flaccid place this Chamber has become under the present government. Oh, there is nothing personal intended as far as the leader of the NDP is concerned. His speech was one of the more coherent I have heard him make in all the years I have been here.

(Mr. Nielsen.]
an imaginative program of building roads, bridges and other means of communication. I recall the words of the next prime minister of that day charging us with spending money like drunken sailors. He charged us with building roads from igloo to igloo in the north. The government of that day made a fair number of yards in southern Canada with that kind of accusation, yet one of the roads, indeed the specific road criticized by the Liberal prime minister of that day as being from igloo to igloo, was the self same Dempster highway that we are discussing in this debate today.
This was a road which was commenced in 1958, 80 miles of which were constructed by 1963 when the government changed. Immediately construction of the road ceased. It was the philosophy of the government of that day that there were oil reserves in the north which would benefit Canadians. That was the philosophy behind the commencement of the construction of that particular road. We were charged with wasting money, so construction of that road was halted in 1963. After the discovery of oil in Prudhoe Bay the government belatedly recommenced construction of the road and now, all of a sudden, it has become one of the most important links in the route to the Arctic which, I am certain, will eventually tap Canadian reserves of gas and oil in the Arctic.
We are speaking not only of gas in the Delta but of oil in the Yukon, oil in the Yukon, oil in the Eagle plain and in the Peel plateau. I do not know whether the President of the Privy Council has any idea where these places are; I doubt very much whether he has ever been to the north. I would invite him to the north, as I would invite the hon. gentleman who is now his colleague who is seated beside him. Let him come to the Yukon and have a look. I know the hon. gentleman has been to Inuvik. Now being a member of the cabinet he is obviously expressing the view of the government when he says that there must be a pipeline. At this stage I could do no better than to quote something to arouse the memories of some of the hon. members here who might remember their history. I am referring to Lord Durham's Report wherein he said:
The colonistsand we in the Yukon are still colonistsmay not always know what laws are best for them or which of their countrymen are the fittest for conducting their affairs; but at least they have a greater interest in coming to a right judgment on these points and will take greater pains to do so than those whose welfare is very remotely and slightly affected by the good or bad legislation of these portions of the Empire.
That is what is being done here, and that is what the Leader of the New Democratic Party is attempting to do in his own self-effacing fashion when he stated that we know better here what decisions to impose on the people of the Yukon.
One of the conditions which is attached to building any pipeline through the Yukon is that all of these factors, which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) has referred to, the parliamentary secretary who has just resumed

his seat and the Leader of the New Democratic Party have also referred to, are essential, and should be decided by the people of the Yukon Territory through their duly elected legislative assembly.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) has always advanced two arguments. The hon. members from the province of Quebec should understand what I am speaking about when we call for maitres chez-nous. He has said that you cannot have autonomy "until you have the people and the money to pay for it. As long as we in the federal treasury are paying, then we are going to call the tune." Thus you are left with the argument of people.
Since when has the establishment of democratic institutions depended upon a target level of people for its functions? The problems which confront the people of the Yukon in the construction of a pipeline can be best solved by themselves. I hear various well-intentioned criticisms by southerners. There are those who advocate no pipeline at all. There are those who advocate a delay in the pipeline, which is simply asking for the delay of a future crisis in the supply of fuels to southern Canada. These are simply not in line.

The article was written in 1966 by R. A. J. Phillips, who is now with Heritage Canada. The article was entitled "The Story of the Yukon and Northwest Territories" and reads in part as follows:
The Yukon will not look like parts of southern Canada where towns and cities are joined by farms, and highways are dotted with villages. Between the northern towns, the Yukon will remain unchanged, its plains, its rivers, its mountains as majestic as when the land was born. And its rocks and gravels will, as in the past, quicken the hearts and hopes of men.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF PROPOSALS FOR NORTHERN GAS PIPELINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have two questions to decide tonight and tomorrow: first, do we need a gas pipeline now; and second, what route should we adopt?
Reviews of our production, consumption and demand for all kinds of energy show our Canadian oil demand to be 2,670 million barrels yearly. Our daily production is 1,780,000 barrels and our imports are 890,000 barrels. We export 918,000 barrels. We produce 2,520 million cubic feet of gas annually. We use 1,000,348,000 ourselves and we export 946 million cubic feet. We also produce 273 billion kilowatts of electricity

in total annually, which is 26.6 per cent of our total energy production. So far only 1.4 per cent is nuclear. Coal, coke and natural gas in turn supply 26.1 per cent of our energy supply.
The export of oil to the United States has been reduced by one half since 1975. The natural gas export to the United States has also been reduced markedly. Both of these are on contracts which we must respect, and we are able to exchange other forms of energy in return for our exports. This mainly consists of coal for our Ontario Hydro. We are now importing oil for energy use, particularly for the Canadian regions east of the Ottawa valley line, from the OPEC countries. It used to be one million barrels daily and is now approximately 300,000 to 400,000 barrels a day.
Canada is doing research and demonstration projects on renewable resources such as on winds, sun, tides, and the biomass. It is conceded that these are most unlikely to become practical total substitutes for our fossil fuels but certainly are adjunctive. When petroleum, gas and coal run out, our energy will have to come in the main from hydro, nuclear installations, and the biomass.
Nuclear power will need fast development, particularly in Ontario, because in this province we are losing the self-sufficiency we once enjoyed in energy. Dr. Rasmussen of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology stated that nuclear power is the safest, cheapest and cleanest form of energy production. Even now breeder reactors for atomic fusion are being built in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Russia. The most recent is the super Phoenix in France. It was the scene of an incited anti-nuclear mob recently, which I.deplore. None of these will be able to rival Canada's CANDU reactor because of their complexity and the need to find new metallic transducers or mediators to replace the light water. Our CANDU heavy water reactor can be adapted to the new Canadian concept of a breeder reactor. It will adopt the thorium cycle. This will make our present uranium resources stretch out 50 times further. It will also permit the use of the very poor grades of uranium, which are so plentiful in the earth's crust. This will make civilization many hundreds of years down the energy road.
From all accounts of economists, geologists, as well as oil and gas companies and government information sources, we will run into an acute energy scarcity around the year 1980. This will continue until the year 1986, at least. That is why we are striving so hard to become self-sufficient in Canadian-produced energy. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has frequently stated, there is no guarantee that Middle East oil will be available until we become self-sufficient. A sudden political upset there could mean that Canada might run into worse shortages than the U.S.A. experienced last winter. For this reason alone we cannot vacillate any longer on the pipeline question.
In fact, as stated in the "Energy Strategy for Canada" our future depends on the synchronization of all our energy modalities. Development of all our gas fields with vigorous
August 4, 1977

exploration for new deposits are imperative. Then Delta and Arctic gas and oil will be set to flow after Alberta oil and gas are exhausted. The tarsands, though expensive, will also be brought into great production. It behooves us to invest heavily in these future energy industries, both privately and publicly.
We may eventually, not only need new pipelines from the Delta and Arctic islands but we may, of necessity, look forward to ice-breaking cargo ships for transportation to carry liquefied Arctic island gas to the St. Lawrence Gulf.
New technologies for lowering the costs of tarsands oil, as well as for Alberta and Saskatchewan coal, are being produced even now. This, we hope, taken all together, will avert any catastrophe which any sudden Middle East boycott could produce. Along with all this necessarily simultaneous development, new oil and gas policies are to be phased in as they become economic or desirable. All that is in the "Energy Strategy for Canada". I wish hon. members would read it.
The government has laid on a very impressive conservation policy for energy. This includes home insulation stimulation throughout the country, the eventual mandatory conversion of private automobiles to low consumption types, and the possible strict rationing of gasoline in the future. There will have to be a planned diversion of fossil fuel energy for public use on railroads and highways, as well as airways and for the manufacture of plastics.
Part of our overview of the construction of pipelines will necessarily include the needs of the U.S. Her oil and gas fields in the lower 48 states are pretty depleted, although she is getting new supplies from the Gulf of Mexico and to some extent from her offshore Atlantic areas. Prudhoe Bay in Alaska has added 10 per cent to her inventory with both its gas and oil. One of her big hopes is that she can get supplies for her carry-over period from Mexico, which country may soon enter an enlarged exporting phase.
Prudhoe Bay oil has already begun to flow to Valdez and transportation to the upper western U.S. refineries will soon begin. This carries some danger to our Canadian coastal waters from pollution. It also presents the U.S. with the need to build more pipelines across its wide range of mountains to the mid-western states. It became obvious to them that a gas pipeline which requires gas-liquefaction after arriving at Valdez from the north slope and special new ships to transport it to the U.S. mainland, followed by more pipelines to the midwest, was anything but economical.
Both Canada and the U.S. know that Prudhoe Bay is a much cheaper and more efficient route by going down to Fairbanks, diverting to Dawson and Whitehorse in the Yukon, and finally running across upper B.C. and Alberta. The originally well researched plan of the Canadian Arctic Gas consortium along the Alaska-Yukon corridor to the Mackenzie Delta and then down the Mackenzie River would have been slightly easier but has certain ecological and socio-economic disadvantages.
We can argue for the CAGPL that it was a consortium made up of U.S. and Canadian companies, that it had consid-
Northern Gas Pipeline
erable experience from its background companies, and that it seemed to have a good prospect of raising plenty of money. However, against the CAGPL submission, as seen by the NEB and by the report of Justice Berger, there are several black marks.
The consortium was fairly strong in their insistence for a government guarantee. We Canadians feel that a trans-Canada pipeline of this sort should be built privately by Canadians and, as it were, rented to the U.S. Justice Berger was very vocal in castigating the CAGPL plan. He ruled out the pipeline from Prudhoe Bay to the Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula along the Alaska-Yukon corridor because of the possibility of extinguishing the caribou herds, the migratory birds, the furbearing animals, and even the whales in the Beaufort Sea which calve on this nearby Arctic shore. He felt very strongly that the opinions of the Inuit, Indian and Metis peoples could not be circumvented. He stated that there would be a socioeconomic black-out perpetrated and, just as important, he asked for a ten year moratorium and for the land claims to be settled.
I cannot agree that we should have a moratorium on any northern line for ten years because we will need the gas from that area in not more than five or ten years. So if that is the case, we will have to build some pipeline with this in view and start very shortly as the construction time is five to six years from planning. I was not convinced after an Arctic tour that the corridor plan would be very harmful ecologically.
A few separate points should be examined. Can we take on the $5 billion to $10 billion dollar investment in a pipeline and still find enough capital to allow further industrial development in Canada such as mining, nuclear reactor building, tidal power, transportation improvement, and the heavy cost of our system of social security?
Looking at it one way, there is no doubt the injection of this amount of money into Canada would be a stimulant to recovery in our economy. It would provide employment for many tradesmen, as well as labourers, and enhance the development of technology in many lines. There would be an impressive spin-off in many other lines of manufacturing and industry generally. It would bring temporary prosperity to the native population, with some hope for local industry in the future.
Dr. Peters, vice-president of the Toronto Dominion Bank, has given a good overview of this economic situation and shows that with ordinary growth in the next 13 years, we will double or triple our GNP and have plenty of capital left over for the other uses even after completing the pipeline. This does not preclude offshore borrowing, privately and publicly. In fact he is reassuring when he says that the amount of offshore borrowing would not appreciate in the next 13 years and we would generate enough capital from our own savings to promote all these expenditures in that period.
Furthermore, there are the completion dates to think of. The CAGPL, if started late this year, could be finished in 1981, that is, before we actually think our production scarcity will begin. The new ALCAN route could be completed by 19831984. This also gives Canada the option to begin the Dempster

With care, good planning and decisive action we can obtain our much needed pipeline and still live up to our contractual obligations to our neighbours in the U.S.A., and to our own northern Canadians. We have many great issues facing us in this country at the present time. They all need a solution. The building of a pipeline is just as necessary in keeping Canada together as is our handling of the Quebec problem. The benefits for Canada seem to outweigh the costs. Some of the benefits are employment, economic activity and the opening of the Yukon. This might be the boost the Canadian economy needs because of the state it is left in by the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite for the last four or five years. This pipeline will require the manufacture of pipe and other activities. It will help the foreign exchange situation. There may be tax revenue, and there is a possibility that this route may provide a chance for us to bring Delta gas through the Dempster Highway link. In our opinion all these things would make it worth while for the government to go ahead with a decision to proceed with the Alcan route as approved by the NEB.
This would be taking two gambles, but they seem to be safe on the face of it. The Dempster Highway link from the Delta will be feasible in an economic sense as well as feasible in an environmental sense. The Dempster Highway would be a great benefit as a result of this project. The rest of the benefits would only be benefits for the next four or five years. Second, our need for frontier gas from the Delta or the Beaufort Sea will not come until the last half of the 1980's. We can get by without frontier gas until then.
Our position-certainly my feeling-is that the government should advise the United States that it is ready to go ahead under the conditions our leader outlined today. I do not see why these conditions should have to be negotiated. We should offer the Americans this route subject to these reasonable conditions, and the Americans can either accept them or use their alternative, which is to liquefy natural gas from Alaska and bring it by ship to California or wherever.
I do not like what I see and hear. I have in my hand an article from today's newspaper. The headline is "Ottawa Appears to be Jittery on Yukon Pipeline Commitment". The article refers to an attack of last minute jitters in the Canadian government. We saw that here this afternoon at the end of the question period. The ministry was pretty jittery. The government is jittery also because of the frosty reception it encountered last week in Washington when Mr. Basil Robinson and his team of negotiators went down there. The Americans did not fall over them and say, "Thank God you will be giving us the Alcan route". The Americans said they would not accept a number of things. They say they may not agree to an all-events tariff which would be necessary unless there are going to be government guarantees in connection with this pipeline. If, because of our good neighbourliness, we are prepared to give to the United States a route across Canada for a gas pipeline subject to conditions which are reasonable to Canadians, Yukoners and people who would live along the route, and if the United States is not prepared to accept those reasonable conditions, then let us forget it. Mr. Speaker, during this debate 1 want to make a few observations about the north and its people. Perhaps this will be a diversion from what we have heard earlier. I should say at the outset that 1 do not recall an issue on which there has been more information over a prolonged period of time than that surrounding the present debate. The divergent views expressed on a multitude of interrelated issues is one manifestation of the complexity and importance of the subject.
In assessing the information, it has been my impression that the participants involved collect information from their own perspective, and the strategy to disseminate that information varies from that of retaining a narrow point of view to retaining a narrow point of view while giving the appearance of a broader perspective of the issues. I do not say this in a critical manner; indeed it is my belief we have been exposed to a new decision making process in dealing with an important and sensitive political issue.
The question must be asked: is there a common denominator, is there a starting point from which we can reconcile the divergent opinions that surround the present debate? 1 suspect the simple answer to that question is no, and yet it seems to me there are convincing arguments to suggest all northerners- and I emphasize all northerners-are telling us they are concerned about individual freedom and equality of opportunity.
The irony of this debate is that the Liberal government would have the House of Commons and the Canadian public believe that by permitting members of parliament to speak for a period of two days the words of wisdom flowing from all concerns of the House will lead to more enlightened decisions. However, what is obvious and what the government has failed

to tell the Canadian people is that many of the issues involved in the debate have been ignored by the Liberal government for years and have been permitted to fester like an untreated chronic ulcer. The illusion created by the government that we are simply debating a pipeline is spurious, and has had the serious and unfortunate effect of diverting attention away from many of the critical political issues which affect the north.
What are some of the issues that have a direct impact on the north, its people and their future, that have been ignored or inadequately handled by the government? The absence of a national energy policy has been discussed earlier today, in particular the long term need for Canada, in concert not only with the western world but with the global community, to rationalize our future energy needs. Despite widely conflicting reports with respect to existing and potential petroleum resources in Canada, it is generally accepted that there is a need for a transition strategy toward a different kind of energy economy. The importance of such a strategy on decisions affecting northern development and Canadian sovereignty over a disproportionate share of the world's territory and resources is obvious.
The absence of a comprehensive policy for the north, the absence of an industrial development strategy and a national policy regarding resource development, has a direct impact on the future of the north and its people. What will be the role of Petro-Canada? The conflicts between the federal and provincial governments, between provincial governments, and the conflicting objectives between various federal ministries and indeed within specific ministries, including the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, have created uncertainty, stagnation, and inaction. The political development of the north and the role of native northerners in that development process is crucial, and I shall make reference to this point later.
Any rational discussion about the future of the north and its people must be predicated on our past and present knowledge of the area and its people. Following several visits to the north and innumerable discussions with a broad cross section of northerners, one is left with definite impressions. Indeed for many reasons which I do not have time to discuss there is a growing awareness of the north in southern Canada, which in itself is healthy, and as one Canadian interested in the future of the north and its people I would like to make a few observations.
1 believe it is fair to say that the north during its three centuries of contact with the white man has been viewed by those in southern Canada as a sparsely populated, hostile environment, with vast natural resources that should serve as a resource base for the rest of Canada and the world.
Although the nature of the resources has changed through the centuries, the basic principle of exploitation of natural resources in the north independent of the economic, social and political development of the area has been and continues to be the policy of this government. Indeed in recent years the state has been involved in numerous projects to the extent that there
August 4, 1977

is no apparent difference in the activities in the public as distinguished from the private sector. The question is not whether these resources should be developed now or in the future, but rather how they should be developed, over what period of time, with what safeguards and for whose benefit?
I am convinced this policy of exploitation is regressive. It is essential that the Canadian north be respected on its own terms, and future policy must be adopted to acknowledge the special characteristics of the north and the culture of its people.
The second point I wish to make is the lack of understanding that prevails regarding the impact our society has had on the economic, social and political development of the Indian, Inuit and Metis in the north. In assessing the impact there is a risk of either accepting de facto the interpretation of the events as perceived by a particular group, or a risk of becoming paralyzed by a number of widely divergent interpretations from several groups based on their perception of events. It is essential to make a distinction between the opinions of the various parties and the necessity to have an understanding of the events which have occurred.
To draw an analogy, it could be compared to three patients visiting a doctor with similar symptoms, where the first patient was convinced he had leukemia, the second cancer, and the third meningitis. The doctor has the choice of treating each patient as they have interpreted the symptoms, or attempt to elicit the facts and draw his own conclusions.
What are the facts? During the past 30 years there has been a remarkable shift in the Canadian economy from a goods producing system to a services producing system. During this period we have seen a growing portion of our economic resources allocated to health care, communications, transportation, education, and social services. This growth in the service sector has been accompanied by changes in financing, in which many of the services formerly financed in the private sector are now the responsibility of the public sector.
There is no question these changes have had a dramatic impact on the traditional way of life in the north. With the continued high birth rate, improved health standards and decreasing mortality rates, we are witnessing the highest population increase on record. Added to this is a marked reduction of previous nomadic activity. The results of these events have been an explosion in the population and the establishment of more permanent settlements.
Not unexpectedly this sequence of events has been accompanied with problems in housing, lack of infrastructure, unemployment, and the numerous social problems one would anticipate in such an environmental setting. In recent years there have been an increasing number of children attending schools in the north, and one cannot escape the inevitable question of asking about their future. Will we be able to provide them with a life style of their choice? Having provided them with the educational equipment to work in a wage economy, will we be able to provide them with the economic opportunities in
Northern Gas Pipeline
their communities? Will conditions be such that their future opportunities are limited, causing a further breakdown in families as children are forced to leave home to seek opportunities elsewhere, most likely in the provinces?
I do not underestimate the difficulties in achieving the proper balance in reconciling the divergent views which exist regarding the future economic, social, and political evolution of the north. However, I am confident if we understand the past, and if there is a commitment to the future, we can achieve the proper balance which will preserve individual freedom and equality of opportunity.
In the brief time remaining I should like to make a few comments regarding the first volume of Mr. Justice Berger's Report and native land claims in the north. Few doubt the eloquent report of Justice Berger has had a significant impact on those preoccupied with the problems of native land claims, economic development and political evolution in the north. Although it is too early to assess the effect the Berger inquiry will have on the future political climate in Canada, it is important to understand the significance of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline inquiry.
It seems clear from the proceedings of the Berger inquiry and a review of the testimony collected, either from informal gatherings in small settlements in the north or larger centres with exposure to the news media in the south, that the future of people was the dominant theme. Although I am not in agreement with all of the conclusions of Justice Berger, I am persuaded to conclude he has added an important dimension to the decision-making process of assessing development projects. In contrast to the James Bay hydro power project in northern Quebec, when the people were forgotten prior to the injunction to stop the development, the Berger inquiry recognized the need to establish the effect development would have on the people in the north. Historically economic concerns dominate the decision-making process in assessing development. Justice Berger has provided a source of information expressing other concerns, and this fundamental principle should be recognized as an important component in any technology assessment program applied to future development.
During the debate on second reading of the James Bay legislation I attempted to define some of the difficulties encountered in resolving the important issue of comprehensive land claims in the north. I emphasized the need for flexibility since no one, in my opinion, in our democratically constituted society has the wisdom or foresight to predict how an individual or a people will evolve. On the basis of the existing proposals or stated objectives of the Northwest Territory Indian Brotherhood, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, the Committee for Original Peoples Entitlement, the Metis principally around Great Slaves Lake and the Delta, and the Council for Yukon Indians, the need for flexibility continues to exist.
The flexibility does not imply inaction. Indeed the major components of comprehensive land claims are well known, and yet the government had failed to acknowledge the reality of northern native aboriginal claims and has refused to come to grips with this fundamental issue.

Unfortunately the time constraints imposed by the House prevent me from outlining the details of the various proposals. However, at the risk of generalizing, it should be noted there is a remarkable similarity in the major components of the proposals that have been presented to the government, which I believe the majority of Canadians would accept in principle. I want to conclude my remarks by referring to what I consider to be the major issue in Mr. Justice Berger's report, and perhaps in the entire debate, namely his reasoning for imposing a ten year moratorium on the building of a pipeline. Let me attempt to place the problem in perspective by initially quoting from the first volume where he states at page 174 the following:
Local, regional or territorial political entities may evolve that have a predominantly native electorate, an electorate in which a native majority might be entrenched by a suitable residency clause. Or political instruments may be developed by which the native people can, under an ethnic franchise and within a larger political entity, control matters that are, by tradition and right, theirs to determine. One approach would be geographical, the other functional.
Again, at page 176, he states:
The settlement of native claims must be the point of departure for any political reorganization in the Northwest Territories. That is why the decision on the pipeline is really a decision about the political future of the Northwest Territories.
In a recent submission to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) the Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories proposed the division of the Northwest Territories into three sections on ethnic grounds. Indeed in an earlier proposal to the federal government they stated:
There will therefore be within Confederation, a Dene government with jurisdiction over a geographical area and over subject matters now within the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada or the government of the Northwest Territories.
The issue is quite clear. If one supports the moratorium for the reasons outlined by Justice Berger, one is in effect supporting the principle of separate national development on ethnic grounds, in other words a homeland policy as proposed in South Africa, and perhaps it is not coincidental the title of the first volume is in part referred to as "Northern Homeland".
What are the implications of accepting the Dene proposal for political independence on the basis of race and culture, which appears to be supported in Judge Berger's recommendations?
First is the assumption that the federal government has not, cannot, and will not be trusted to administer an obligation under the B.N.A. Act to protect the interests and rights of the Indian people. This point of view has its proponents in both the north and south, among Indians and non-Indians, for a variety of reasons. Some are prisoners of the past, others are romanticists, and others espouse personal ideologies with questionable credentials regarding their genuine interest in resolving Indian problems.
If a federal government accedes to the request for independence, we are admitting as a nation and more important, as a

people, that we do not have the capacity and flexibility to adapt to existing circumstances, and we are admitting independence is an acceptable alternative to the development and respect which can serve to unite us for the mutual benefit of all Canadians.

Although the constitution does not define in a precise manner how the federal government should discharge its responsibilities, it is quite clear action can and should be taken. We need to assist the Indian people to preserve their identity and permit them to choose a way of life in keeping with their cultural heritage. We need to provide the Indian people with the opportunity to build an economic base to ensure the survival of their culture. With respect to political development, we must recognize the importance of Indian involvement in the decision making process, and it seems to me a broad spectrum of possibilities exists other than independence.
Finally, it is impossible to divorce the issue of independence on racial and cultural grounds in the north from the issue of national unity and the future of Canada.
Special status for the Indian people is an integral part of our constitution which must be preserved and continually altered to allow the Indian people the opportunity to preserve their identity and break the shackles of dependency. I believe this is just and attainable.
However, I have not been persuaded that Justice Berger's reasoning will stand the test of time, and to add tacit approval to the Dene proposal for independence supports a fundamental problem that exists in Canada, namely, the notion that a people must be the absolute masters of all matters affecting them.
An important feature of our federal system is that if there is the will it can respond to changing circumstances. As I indicated earlier, to accept independence as a viable option is to admit as Canadians we do not have the capacity and flexibility to adapt to existing circumstances.
It is my belief that federalism and national unity are a viable option over independence, and to take any course of action which accepts in principle the establishment of political independence based on race and culture is to indicate our loss of faith in federalism and our future as an united country. I am a Canadian and stand for a united Canada.

In view of the increasing concern of veterans and their organizations over the number of widows who do not receive pensions, and in view of the increasing concern over the widening gap between the rate of the disability pension and the base to which it was attached a few years ago, as well as the minister's sympathetic statements made several times to the effect that this matter is being reviewed, will he do his best to get the members of the cabinet to agree to bringing in this year the necessary legislation to correct these two situations?
The reply of the minister was in these words:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has indicated, this is a concern of mine and many people in the House. As far as trying to get it implemented this year, I will do my best.
It could well be that this is the last night in this session in which there will be late shows. I know of no subject to which I would rather devote my last effort in an adjournment debate than this one.
I appeal as strongly as I can to the Minister of Veterans Affairs to do what I asked him to do on June 29, as well as on other occasions, to try and get the cabinet to agree to include in the Speech from the Throne that may well be read by Her Majesty in October at least these two matters respecting Canadian veterans.

speechtext: Not just for study.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-NUMBER OF WIDOWS NOT RECEIVING PENSIONS AND LOW LEVEL OF DISABILITY PENSION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
The hon. member is right. We do not want just study, we want action. I realize that every time we discuss the question of pensions for widows of veterans, the minister makes the point that if a veteran's disability pension was only 5 per cent, say, for flat feet, that amount of money would hardly be the main element in the income of that veteran and his wife and that therefore a case for a widow's pension in that situation is not as strong as it might be. I point out to the minister-and he knows it as well as the rest of us do-that the pensions of veterans' widows are not on a graduated basis. Either the widow gets the full widow's pension or she gets nothing at all. The crucial point is that 48 per cent level in the case of the veteran's pension.
The minister knows that several responsible bodies such as the Woods commission, the Hermann commission and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs on at least two or if not more occasions, have recommended that there be a graduated scale so that in the case of widows of veterans where the veteran's pension was less than 48 per cent, there could be a pro rata pension. This is one of the matters that is concerning veterans greatly, and as the years roll on, especially now for World War II veterans as they rolled on some time ago for World War I veterans, the numbers of veterans' widows who do not qualify for pension as a matter of right is increasing, and this is an issue of great concern to veterans. It is being expressed by the veterans in literally every veterans' organization.
I do not think I have to argue with the minister the strength of the case. I think he agrees with it just as strongly as the rest of us do. The problem is to get it approved by the cabinet, to
80020-46'/2

August 4, 1977
Adjournment Debate
get it into the Speech from the Throne, and to get it on the list of legislation for the next session. I plead with him as strongly as 1 can to see to it that it is on that list when we come back into session in October of this year.
The other point covered in my question is another of the major issues that are still of concern to veterans. A few years ago we corrected a wrong that had persisted for nearly 50 years, namely, that the war disability pension lost its relationship to the base to which it was established back in the early 1920's. A few years ago we attached it to a base, namely, the average income after taxes of five categories in the public service. But in the four or five years since that base was established, a gap has developed which is now nearly $45 a month or nearly $540 a year. I have the exact figures in front of me. They are a few cents less, but those are roughly the figures. I submit that it is grossly unfair to the veterans, unfair to the government which brought in this proposal, and unfair to the standing committee which recommended it, and I earnestly plead with the minister and express as strongly as I can to him the hope that this too will be in the Speech from the Throne which will open the next session of parliament.
The minister knows, as do all members, that veterans have a particular feeling of attachment to the Crown, and I suspect that the Sovereign, being herself a woman, has a particular interest in women and in widows, and I can think of nothing better to put in the mouth of the Queen when she opens parliament next October than these two matters respecting veterans.
I know the minister agrees that it should be done. I plead with him tonight to give us the assurance that he will do his best to get the agreement of his colleagues in the cabinet on these two important measures affecting the veterans of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-NUMBER OF WIDOWS NOT RECEIVING PENSIONS AND LOW LEVEL OF DISABILITY PENSION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in answering the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on this matter, as I have done in the past. In 1972 it was recognized that some better method of determining the basic amount of disability pension had to be found, and a joint study group on the basic rate of pension was established. This study group had representation from veterans' organizations as well as from the Canadian Pension Commission and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The joint study group recommended that the salary, after tax, of a composite group composed of five classes of unskilled public servants be accepted as the basis on which the disability pension should be based. This was done, and in June, 1973, Bill C-202 was enacted. That bill established the basic rate of pension in relation to five named classes of unskilled public servants. This resulted in an over-all increase of pension at that time of some 24 per cent.
In 1974, 1975 and 1976, because the pension rate was tied to the consumer price index, it was slightly more than it would have been if it had been tied only to the five categories of unskilled public servants.

This year, however, after deduction of income tax the spread between the income of the unskilled public servant and the pensioner has reached the point where the pension rate is $44.72 a month behind that of the composite group of unskilled public servants, approximately $536 a year.
I am aware of the spread between the pension paid to the single 100 per cent pensioner and the control group of five named classes of unskilled public servants. The question of an upward adjustment of pension rates is under serious consideration.
Insofar as payment of pro rata pensions to widows of pensioned veterans is concerned, I have very little to add since a statement was last made on this subject. The suggestion has been made that a widow should receive a pro rata pension if her husband had been in receipt of a disability pension assessed at the rate of 47 per cent or less. This is because if his pension had been assessed at the rate of 48 per cent or more, the surviving dependants would be pensionable. What is sometimes forgotten is that in addition a widow will be pensioned if her husband's death was attributable to service or occurred during wartime regardless of the degree of the assessment of the disability.
The hon. member predicted that if people are in receipt of as little as 1 per cent pension I would make this statement, so I might as well make it. There is an opportunity to receive war veterans allowance if a person's income enables him to do so. The entire matter of veterans benefits-and that includes the basic rate of pension and pro rata benefits for widows-is under constant review by the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Canadian Pension Commission and the other agencies of my ministry to see what changes can be made to improve the lot of veterans and their dependants. Both subjects are of great importance, and when I have something specific to report to the House, I will be more than pleased to do so.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR OPERATION OF SECURITY SERVICES- KNOWLEDGE OF MINISTER OF ALLEGEDLY ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR OPERATION OF SECURITY SERVICES- KNOWLEDGE OF MINISTER OF ALLEGEDLY ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 24 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether he took the position that the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) or the government should be responsible for the activities of the security services of the RCMP. The Prime Minister said that the principle of ministerial responsibility did apply, but he was less direct in indicating what sort of briefings the Solicitor General got from the force.
Since then interesting things have happened. On June 17 the Solicitor General said there would be no inquiry into the RCMP because the Montreal news agency break-in was, to use the Solicitor General's terminology, exceptional and isolated. Then, early in July, a complete reversal occurred. An inquiry was announced. Obviously, to put it in the most charitable way, between the minister and the RCMP there was an obvious failure to communicate. Who is responsible for this information gap or need "not to know"? 1 cannot believe it is totally the fault of the force.
August 4, 1977

A series of solicitors general have obviously been either too lazy, imperceptive or incompetent to become informed and to live up to their parliamentary obligations and traditions. Perhaps, as Shakespeare said, "When ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise". However, under the terms of reference of this inquiry announced last month there is no thrust, even in part, toward exploring the errors-if not of commission, then of omission-of the government or a series of solicitors general.
No, the RCMP is left literally alone to be checked, and nothing is said to any extent about any responsibility of its political masters. I would have expected this minister to have done better in living up to his responsibilities for the force than this. He has focused the inquiry on the RCMP, leaving the responsibility on the force, rather than assessing the degree of blame which ought to be attached to the Solicitor General and his predecessors.
If I may refer briefly to the British North America Act with reference to the responsibility for security services, there is an interesting, possible conflict between federal and provincial jurisdictions as far as the duties of the RCMP are concerned. As everyone knows, the force at one time was a territorial force known as the North West Mounted Police, with headquarters in Regina, which was then in a territory. Once a province was established, it had to enact its own police act, since every province had and has exclusive jurisdiction under section 92(14) of the BNA Act for its administration of justice. The provinces then enforced not only their own laws but those passed by parliament, for example, the Criminal Code and the War Measures Act.
An examination of section 91 of the act reveals significantly that while subsection (7) provides parliament with control over our militia, military and naval services and defence, there is no provision for the national police force, which is understandable in a way, since the administration of justice by parliament is confined by definition to the territories. Yet, when we turn to the RCMP Act we note an interesting conflict. That act passed by parliament, appoints every member of the force a peace officer in all Canada, and its officers ex officio justices of the peace.
The question which comes to mind is, how is it possible for parliament to pass this legislation, when the appointment of peace officers and justices of the peace is in the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. I shall develop this theme when time permits. For the present suffice it to say that the Royal Commission on Security in 1969 stated then that there is no exclusive statutory authority for the security role of the RCMP. In other words the RCMP, lacking parliamentary direction but realizing what was required, had to make its ow'n terms of reference, which the royal commission pointed out as well. That is another indication of lack of backing for our national police force by a series of governments and ministers.
As a step in the right direction I suggest we should consider amending the BNA Act and inserting in section 91(7), in addition to the provisions concerning the militia, military and
Adjournment Debate
naval services and defence, a provision concerning national police and security services. Parliament should then regularize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, after consulting with the provinces, and consider a better legislative foundation for our security services as well.
The minister, using his ministerial responsibility in the full meaning of the term, as I suggested earlier, owes it to the force to make certain that when the RCMP is contracted to a province, its work there shall be in no way unduly restricted. When I see a letter like the one 1 gave the minister today, a letter from an official of the Nova Scotia attorney general's department to a superintendent of the RCMP, instructing that officer to have deleted certain items from a file, items which would appear to be embarrassing to the Crown prosecutor, the same prosecutor whom the official informed the superintendent would be prosecuting the case, I suggest the Solicitor General owes a duty to the force in that respect, as well, to make certain its work is not being hindered. I think Superintendent Christian, the officer involved, is obviously unhappy with that situation, since he wrote three letters in 11 days. I think the minister has some responsibility for checking such a situation which also comes under the broad mantle of ministerial responsibility.
While the force must in the final analysis be responsible to the civil authority and conform as well to certain policies of the provinces to which it is under contract, the force must never be discouraged or brushed aside from certain areas of criminal investigation for reasons that those areas may touch on matters close to government, any government.
The RCMP is a proud, national force, with national standards of law enforcement to maintain. I trust that the Solicitor General, using his ministerial responsibility, will make sure that its mandate to enforce law and order is never impinged upon. I also hope that the government, in particular the Solicitor General, will do as it promised, implement some of the recommendations of Judge Rene Marin. In this way the minister would have better rapport with the force. I should like to see him improve its work conditions and see a more satisfactory and businesslike relationship between this important law enforcement agency and the Parliament of Canada. Until this is done we shall continue to have these unfortunate situations which have precipitated the present RCMP inquiry and which, as I said at the outset, do little credit to the concept of ministerial responsibility, since the force in effect is left holding the bag. All attention is focused on it and none of the responsibility is focused on those ministers who are responsible by definition and law for the force. I trust this matter will be remedied soon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of accountability is not one which the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) or the government simply acknowledges or endorses. It is a concept which is understood as fundamental to the system of parliamentary democracy in Canada. As practised in our system and by the government, it means acceptance of responsibility for the conduct of government and, of course, for the

August 4, 1977
Adjournment Debate
administrative machinery of the Government in Canada, in the sense it involves an obligation not simply to give direction but also to ensure that those directives given are carried out. But as with any other system of responsibility and obligation, it would be too simplistic to believe that the principle of accountability involves exactly the same thing in each of every aspect of its application. There is, at once, a general understanding of the principle and of its reality in practice.
Thus, in some areas of government endeavour one might anticipate, indeed expect, a rigorous form of this principle. In other, different areas of government operations, one equally expects a less controlled exercise of the principle. For example, the over-all system of government in Canada includes the operations of various Crown corporations. The nature of their activities ranges from that of support to Canadian industry active in the international area to the activity of those Crown corporations involved in domestic operations, such as the Canadian National Railways. These corporations have many features similar to private enterprise organizations, and in some cases they compete evenly in and with the private sector. In order to do so, they must be relatively free of direct ministerial involvement. Yet, at the same time, support given them from taxes collected at large demands ministerial control.
At the other end of the scale of government operations are those areas of endeavour which are of such importance to the national well-being that important ministerial involvement is essential. In the areas of regional disparity, employment, health and welfare, responsible ministers must ensure that the direction they request is indeed met and carried out. In such areas the nature of ministerial responsibility for appropriate public service organizational and individual response is critical. No minister of this government would deny his responsibility and that of departmental employees in such circumstances. There is then no question of the government's sense of and support for this principle. It is a principle which I believe has been met by government action.
