speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the heading of my adjournment speech tonight is "The Trudeau Government-Architects of the near destruction of Canada".

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO STOP EXODUS OF CAPITAL TO UNITED STATES-REASON REAL ESTATE DEVELOPERS WILL NOT INVEST IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO STOP EXODUS OF CAPITAL TO UNITED STATES-REASON REAL ESTATE DEVELOPERS WILL NOT INVEST IN CANADA
speechtext:
At the rate we have been going and on the basis of the information which has come forward in the last couple of weeks we shall soon be able to remove the word "near".
On July 25 I addressed a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) with regard to measures he might take to stop the exodus of capital to the United States and inquiring as to the reason for which real estate developers will
[Mr. Railton.l
not invest in Canada. I got a typical Liberal answer. The minister said, in part, that changes costing something over $700 million had been made in favour of the corporate business sector in the budget of March 31 and the government believed that this, combined with a change in the dividend tax credit for business investment in Canada made for a favourable climate.
That is a meaningless answer and it does absolutely nothing to help the economy. If the present trend of business going to the United States continues, within the next five years Canada will have from two million to 2.5 million unemployed and the government's make-work projects will not be able to match the dollars leaving this country. Over 400,000 students are leaving our schools and universities annually, but only 200,000 new jobs are being created annually. Members can see the direction in which we are headed. It is not a question of whether the government could be returned in the next general election. It is a question of whether we can afford to have it continue in office until this parliament comes to an end.
So that I will not be accused of making strictly a partisan speech tonight I want to quote a financial institution and other financial experts throughout Canada and the United States. Economists for the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce have said that, based on their economic indicators, the current slump may continue into next year. So that absolutely nothing will be done for the one million unemployed in this country or about the mass exodus of investment money. A Royal Bank trader blamed it on lack of concern by the federal government. He said that people are waiting for the government to do something. Well, Mr. Speaker, we will be Rip Van Winkles with beards before this government does anything.
The type of answers that we have been receiving from the Prime Minister to the effect that investors will send their money where they will get the best return is an indication of the concern that he has. He tells people that if they cannot get a job in Canada they should go to the United States. The Royal Bank trader also said that the decline could fuel inflation by raising the price of imported goods. A Bank of Commerce economist said that the weakening in their indicator underscores the fragile state of Canada's economic recovery. These are damaging statements, Mr. Speaker.
According to an article in a recent Wall Street Journal issue, the weaker Canadian dollar is a sign that the money markets are telling the Prime Minister that they have even less confidence in his economic management-that should be mismanagement-than in that of the current U.S. administration. The article points out that the Prime Minister's complacency is not shared by many of his fellow Canadians. Canada is not doing so well. Its economy has been tangled up by a government effort to apply compulsory wage and price controls for nearly two years, when we should have had short-term controls as we in the Conservative party proposed. The article goes on to say:
August 4, 1977

While the nation's troubles are frequently attributed to the rise of the Quebec separatists, it would be more accurate to say that the rise of the Quebec separatists is closely related to the country's economic mismanagement.
Individual U.S. states are also opening up offices in the Montreal and Toronto areas and are being funded by the United States economic development administration. For example, the state of Vermont has opened up an office in Montreal to encourage Canadian businesses to move to the United States. The state wanted to be in a position to attract businesses wishing to move from the province of Quebec. They see that there is a lush open market here, and they know that no smart investor or any Canadian business is going to continue to operate in this country.
A number of United States bankers have combined to provide a $500,000 pool so that low interest loans can be offered to firms contemplating relocation to the United States. Furthermore, American towns and cities along the St. Lawrence plan to blitz Ontario with promotional campaigns aimed at luring Canadian industries across the border. Jefferson county and Watertown recently joined forces to open a new $800,000 industrial park which local officials hope to fill with Canadian satellite plants. They already have two, and leads on three others. That is another example of Canadian business and Canadian investors having no faith in Canada or in the present government.
Last year was a banner year for movements to the United States; 44 companies either moved to New York or expanded existing facilities. Twenty-five came from Ontario and 18 from Quebec. They brought in $28.6 million in investment money and created 1,330 new jobs. Canadians are also buying United States realty. For example, there are 17 major complexes being developed with Canadian money throughout the United States.
I would also draw the attention of the House to a most devastating article which I read recently entitled "Drifting along like ship without rudder", which has reference to this government. I want to point out, in closing, that the reason for all these business investors moving out of Canada is the overtaxation and the over-regulation which are confining these businesses to debt, and they can no longer operate in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MEASURES TO STOP EXODUS OF CAPITAL TO UNITED STATES-REASON REAL ESTATE DEVELOPERS WILL NOT INVEST IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised a number of concerns about reports of business investment and, in particular, investment in real property flowing out of Canada and into the United States.
Adjournment Debate
It is always difficult to obtain a clear and up to date perspective on investment flows in any particular business sector. However, it is important to note that investors continue to express confidence in the Canadian economy and the ability to obtain a return on investment in Canada. Thus, for example, total capital movements, unadjusted for seasonal variations, produced a net capital inflow of $810 million during the first quarter of 1977, while new issues of Canadian securities raised $1.4 billion.
Of course it is the case that within the total flow of capital there are movements in both directions, which represent the response of investors to market conditions and opportunities. In certain areas such as real estate development, two or three major projects can represent in themselves very large dollar transactions. However, it is important not to draw premature or unwarranted conclusions based on a limited number of cases.
It is true that we have faced in the last two years an uphill battle to restore the competitiveness of the Canadian economy, which is the prerequisite for sustained investment. That battle has been difficult, but with widespread public support and co-operation the inflation of our costs has been brought to more acceptable levels. Wage settlements have, for example, shown a steady deceleration in the first six months of this year. Negotiated settlements are now showing increases in the first year of the contract in the order of 8 per cent. In the manufacturing sector, first year increases in Canada were down to 7 per cent in the first quarter, falling below the United States increase of 7.8 per cent.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) indicated in his response on July 25, the budget of March 31 provided additional assistance to equity investment and business finance in Canada, particularly through the increased dividend tax credit, the enriched investment tax credit, and additional measures to assist small business. With the rather cautious case of the current expansion, the full impact of those measures has yet to be felt; but there are encouraging signs of strengthening export markets, particularly in the United States. However, what is important is that we persist in the effort to hold the line on our costs if we wish to ensure the attractiveness of the Canadian economy to investors. That is why the government attaches importance to obtaining agreement with business and labour on wage and price restraint for the period after controls are lifted.
